But it still exploits the lingering Bourdain brand name to the fullest extent, even if Bourdain himself probably wouldn’t have looked twice at this place. In fact, he almost certainly would have scoffed at its signature dessert, the Dubai chocolate cup. Dubai chocolate is the kind of foodie trend that Bourdain would have resented, started or both. Probably both. But he’s no longer here to object, so I order one. Plus the Bourdain shake.Article continues below this adThat shake that bears Bourdain’s name — which includes Biscoff cookies and Biscoff syrup and is topped with Biscoff cookie crumbles — would definitely please his audience. But it’s the Dubai cup that ends up being the best thing I eat at either Shawa establishment. It’s a plastic cup filled with fresh cut strawberries and then topped with Belgian chocolate, pistachio cream and shredded phyllo dough. I had to fight with my digestive system to make room for this thing, but I end up bottoming out the cup in minutes. Dubai chocolate may be a cliche at this point, but this cup isn’t. And if Tony wouldn’t have liked it, that’s not really my concern. I get to do the Sam’s Burger journey my way, which Bourdain himself would have gleefully encouraged. There’s a fine line between inspiration and imitation, and I know which of the two he preferred.Bourdain died eight years ago and has remained beloved ever since. But enough time has passed now for his immediate memory to begin fading from the public consciousness. In place of the man and his work — his books, his television shows, his restaurant recommendations — there’s a lasting, eat-drink-and-be-merry philosophy that his name now connotes. As such, you and I are living through Anthony Bourdain’s transition from mourned celebrity to something closer to an icon: the kind of historic figure who endures more as an ideal than as anything else. Tony, to use only his first name, is posthumously becoming the Elvis of food and drink. You can see that transition happening for yourself at Sam’s and at Legends. More importantly, you can taste it.Article continues below this ad

item.title: Why Your Team Sucks 2026: San Francisco 49ers
item.content:encoded: Some people are fans of the San Francisco 49ers. But many, many more people are NOT fans of the San Francisco 49ers. This 2026 Defector NFL team preview is for those in the latter group. Read all the previews so far at Defector.: San Francisco 49ers.Article continues below this ad: 12-5. You wanna get to the part about the owner being too horny for the law, so I’ll blow through this section as fast as is responsible. The 2025 49ers were a shining example of how a football team can prosper in the face of adversity. And by “adversity,” I mean half its roster tearing a ACL, its highest paid receiver contracting whatever mental illness Kanye West has, and prolonged exposure to Mac Jones. I’d award the Niners some sort of medal for their fortitude, but they got rinsed by Seattle in the divisional round so f—k that.San Francisco’s first loss of 2025 occurred against Jacksonville, after which then-defensive coordinator Robert Saleh and Jags head coach Liam Coen got extra spicy with one another at midfield after the final whistle, in the familiar “these guys are just competitors” kind of way. The Niners also got waxed by Tampa Bay during one of Baker Mayfield’s brief dalliances with MVP-level level quarterbacking, as shown in this highlight. Great coverage on that play.The LA Rams avenged an early OT loss to the Niners by beating the unholy s—t out of them in Santa Clara. Then Seattle beat them in their house in the final week of the season to clinch the top seed in the NFC. HOWEVER, the Niners still managed to bravely qualify for the playoffs despite all of that, and despite the following injuries:Article continues below this adEDGE Nick Bosa: Torn ACL (his racism tendon thankfully remains healthy and intact)LB Fred Warner: Dislocated and broken ankleRookie DE Mykel Williams: Torn ACLWR Ricky Pearsall: Something about a PCL (he’s already out for all of this coming season)WR Brandon Aiyuk: Nasty case of the insanesRB Christian McCaffrey: Brutally murdered in a standoff with local police (NOTE: This did not happen)Tight end George Kittle would tear his Achilles in a wild card victory over Philadelphia, thus completing the (leg) sweep. And while it was thrilling to watch the 49ers’ remaining skeleton crew beat Philly on the road, the Niners only won that game because the Eagles are catty meatheads who live for the drama. A trip to Seattle in the divisional round set things in their proper order, and from the opening kickoff.San Francisco never threatened after that. If they had, they probably would have slipped on a banana peel and impaled themselves on a sprinkler head. The Seahawks would go on to win the Super Bowl a month later, in the Niners’ home stadium.Got all that? Good, now let’s get to the asshole parade.Article continues below this ad: Kyle Shanahan. You know how football coaches will sometimes run wind sprints with players so that they can be like, “You see? I’m willing to suffer just like you guys!” Well, Kyle did those coaches one better this summer when he was like, “I always subject my players to catastrophic injuries, so it’s only fair that I horribly maim myself!” Shanny’s chosen method of hurticide was to wreck the unholy s—t out of his Tesla. This act of solidarity netted the coach a concussion, several broken ribs, a broken nose, a broken hand, a busted eye, and an unfortunate mustache. This is the one time in history when it would have been safer to have Aldon Smith behind the wheel.How on earth did Kyle crash his car so bad? Well, turns out he’d put the ol’ girl on autopilot mode so he that could check his phone, at which point his Model Firestarter X crossed into the adjacent lane and bashed into another car.“I’ve had autopilot for nine years, so I’m pretty comfortable with it and, you know, who knows what happened when I turned around? Whether it malfunctioned or whether I knocked it off? That’s something I don’t know yet,” he said.YOU’RE NOT SUPPOSED TO LET THE CAR DRIVE FOR YOU, YOU F—KING IDIOT. Yes, who knows what happened when you deliberately stopped looking where your car was going? What were you supposed to do, NOT check your phone while driving? What is this, Soviet Russia?Article continues below this adI drove by the crash site in question last week. No lie. I was there in person. The intersection of Alma and Hamilton in Palo Alto is block away from an awkward, very dangerous interchange with University Avenue. It’s a hairy bit of driving even when your eyes are fixed on the road, but this perennial dickhead was like, “Ooh, this is the perfect spot for me to check all the Flock cameras I had mounted outside every player’s house!” And the cops let Kyle walk! And the press sat on the story for nearly two weeks! And yet this man has the gall — the pure, unmitigated GALL — to publicly say “my bad” after news of the crash finally broke? Man f—k you, Kyle. You’re no stand-up guy. You’re a “sit in your Elonmobile and let it plow into a 21-year-old woman who was just trying to make a food run” guy. F—k you and your s—tty car.Saleh left this coaching staff to go be fired by the Titans in two years. Your new DC is former tragic Falcons decision Raheem Morris. Your new offensive coordinator is one of the Kubiaks. And guess who else joined the staff this offseason?Maybe that car wreck really did leave Kyle blind.Article continues below this ad: Brock Purdy, who is very good but is absolutely not built for this s—t. Purdy has missed time every season, and not merely because he plays for the injury factory. With an aging roster around him — not to mention a corps of pass-catchers who continually step in bear traps on their way to take a piss — Purdy now has to shoulder much more of the Niners’ offensive load than he did back when he was a charming Mr. Irrelevant story. That Brock Purdy was a wee little sweetcheeks who captivated hearts all across the nation right up to the second his elbow snapped like a chopstick in the NFC title game. That’s why the Niners kept reasonable Purdy facsimile Mac Jones as their QB2 for this season instead of entertaining lucrative trade offers for the pending free agent (NOTE: No one was gonna trade anything valuable for Mac f—king Jones).: [dominatrix voice] Who’s been a bad little boy?Yes, when you’re a millionaire many times over and your marriage is falling apart, there’s nothing more relaxing than hitting up an Ohio trailer park to buy a cheap nut. But UH OH, JED YORK! Turns out that classified ad you saw promising a magical $140 romp with a lady of the night was an op!Article continues below this ad"In a 2024 story on the task force, the Ohio AG’s office spotlighted detective Dan Haueter’s work using online ads in prostitution stings: 'Catching rats and other vermin starts with using the right bait, and when Det. Haueter sets the trap, they come scurrying.'" www.sfgate.com/49ers/articl...[image or embed]— Grant Marek (@grantmarek.bsky.social) August 25, 2026 at 12:31 PMAs you can see, law enforcement in Ohio really has its priorities straight. Do I wish that state would focus its law enforcement resources on mass gun violence, hate crimes, corporate malfeasance, and other, much more pressing issues? Yes. Am I glad they chose to humiliate an NFL owner instead? Also yes. The bodycam video of York’s arrest is worth watching if only to see what York was wearing while on his way to get some. World’s ugliest Yankees T-shirt? Jogging shorts? White ankle socks and sneakers? (fans self) WHOA HEY I’M GETTING A LITTLE BIT RANDY HERE. This is what my wife orders me to wear to bed on our special date nights.Anyway, it’s morbidly amusing that NFL owners can get away with all manner of f—kery while they’re chilling in the white-collar sector, only to have the human trafficking panic come for them the second they make a side visit to Poortown for a little bit of sin. As with Robert Kraft, York has tried to bury as much evidence of his encounter as possible. And, like Kraft, he’ll probably be suspended from the team raw bar for a period of no less than six hours. After that, he’ll be a free, and definitely repentant, man. All rich men love personal growth!I suppose I should get to the on-the-field stuff regarding this team, so here you go: The Niners’ roster is already pre-deceased. Bosa likely won’t be back for Week 1. Kittle has been activated from the PUP list despite rupturing his Achilles less than eight months ago. Free agent addition WR Mike Evans, who missed most of last season in Tampa Bay with a busted collarbone, is already nursing a bum quad. Mykel Williams is on the PUP list. McCaffrey, already perched on the rim of the age cliff, was held out of camp practices because of “soreness,” maybe because Kyle accidentally ran him over while scrolling Insta at 75 mph. The team’s biggest offseason addition, DT Osa Odighizuwa, had to get his elbow surgically cleaned out in January. Everyone is banged up, and we haven’t even played any real football yet. I think we all know what’s going on here. That’s right: It was the electrical substation, in the Study, with the Lead Pipe. Only viable explanation for why this team can’t stop murdering its own.Article continues below this adThe good news is that rookie WR De’Zhaun Stribling is only kinda sorta hurt. Even better, he’s been getting raves in training camp. Now, we all know that if you’re gassing up rookies in camp, it’s only because you’re f—ked if (when, really) they end up playing like rookies. But have you considered that the powerful substation gamma rays bombarding the 49ers’ practice facility could actually be giving players like Stribling Spider-Man powers? Grok tells me it’s not out of the question, and when has an Elon Musk product ever failed me?More good news: WR Deebo Samuel is back, as is fan favorite LB Dre Greenlaw. Because when Kyle ran back the all-22 from 2025, he said to himself, “This team needs to get even older and more busted.” HEY PRESTO! You’re looking at a potential (2019) juggernaut. Will this team still be able to squeeze 10 wins from a stone? Probably. Will it amount to anything? AHAHAHAHA no. Come on. Don’t be one of those chemtrails people.Jed York moved back to Ohio because he’s mad about California’s new wealth tax. If you think that living in Ohio is worth that much, you don’t deserve to be in charge of a lemonade stand, much less a professional football team.Jauan Jennings left in free agency. They still don’t have a viable left guard on the roster. Al Guido looks like Big Dom’s prosperous brother-in-law.Article continues below this ad: I’m done acknowledging Kyle as one of the best coaches in the NFL, and the NFL media should be, too. They’re always like, “Oh, [generic new head coach somewhere] is from the Kyle Shanahan tree! Kyle is the best play-caller in the sport! He can take his’n and beat your’n!” Meanwhile, the guy is out there blowing playoff games, bugging every inch of team headquarters, and letting Cyberjesus take the wheel every time he gets a push alert. And for what? Jerry Jones has won a Super Bowl more recently than you guys, that’s how distant the 49ers’ glory years are. And you’re not getting anywhere near them again so long as your owner is looking for love in Youngstown and your head coach has hurt more people than Uday Hussein ever did. Accept your forthcoming mediocrity and f—k off out of my sight.: San Francisco is still one of the best cities on the planet. I hope it gets itself an NFL team one day.HEAR IT FROM NINERS FANS!Article continues below this adI was five when the 49ers won their last Super Bowl and have no memory of it.Our biggest rival is an electrical substation.Waking today and seeing Jed York’s mugshot is the happiest this team has made me feel in over 10 years.Kyle Shanahan getting into a horrific car accident because he opted to drive a vehicle that doesn’t need his help to get from point A to point B also perfectly sums up his coaching career.Article continues below this adTheir best WR is having a mental breakdown, Bosa probably injected ivermectin to fix his knee, Seattle is going to destroy us again, and Shanny always wears the dumbest hat he can find all season long. We’re f—ked.Why is everything so weird, man? Why was our coach in a shady, mysterious car accident? Why are 20 players already on the IR, when we haven’t even started playing preseason? Why is half the roster 400 years old? Why is Deebo back (HI DEEBO WE MISSED YOU!)? What is even going on with Brandon Aiyuk and can someone get that dude some help? Did someone hire an Etsy witch? Fess up, Dallas. We know it was you.The vibes are rancid and the hum and rattle of the transformer station conspiracy theories are seeping into the brainpans of our already-challenged fanbase. It’s gonna be a long f—king season.We should have drafted competent doctors and physical therapists. Article continues below this adThis team’s window is sealed tighter than a malfunctioning Cybertruck’s. I hate Nick Bosa more than San Franciscans hate the homeless.In the last 15 years, we have led in the 4th quarter of three Super Bowls, and four additional NFC championship games. All we have to show for it is having to wait longer to hear Drew tell us why we suck every August.I wish Nick Bosa had been riding that scooter instead of Harrison Bader.Shanahan still hasn’t learned to coach when it matters or drive a car like a normal human being. I want a Waymo to run me over so that I don’t have to watch this team anymore.Article continues below this adNick Bosa is a linchpin of our Super Bowl chances and I’m worried this f—king guy might spell linchpin with a y.There is a zero-percent chance Christian McCaffrey will make it through the season and who knows if Mike Evans will have hamstrings once the substation fields get to them.I often think about what this team’s accomplishments could be if everyone involved with running it didn’t have their heads so firmly entrenched up their own asses.I’ve always hated the “Faithful” horses—t. What is it I have faith in, exactly? That by Week 5, all 11 starters will be third and fourth stringers, because the rest of the depth chart met in secret and conspired to all shred their ACLs on the same day? That in the years the team somehow doesn’t collectively fall into a pit full of rusty spikes, Shanny will pull one of his patented 4th-quarter nut-shrivels and piss away a 15-point Super Bowl lead to Patrick Mahomes? That Nick Bosa will show up to every post-game presser in camo and a gaiter, ready to moonlight as an honorary ICE agent?Article continues below this adNow add to that the fact that the world’s largest microwave oven is pointed straight at the practice field, slowly cooking everybody’s insides to the consistency of cat meat, and our coach has such a severe TBI that James Taylor sounds like Metallica, and attempting to hold two ideas in his brain at one time makes his head spin like Regan in “The Exorcist.” And you can’t even feel sorry for the poor bastard, because it’s his own damn fault for driving like a teenager with a Snapchat addiction.Also, our fans are a f—king embarrassment. No fans are worse than those in Philly, Dallas, and Boston, but somehow we have crawled right down into the sewer with them. The rare times I venture among them online, I find it so humiliating I feel like Cersei on her walk of shame through King’s Landing. Sorry, JimmyBangBang81 from Redwood City, Brock isn’t elite and he never will be. Shouting ALL-CAPS at Steven Ruiz on Twitter will not make it so. Please just shut the f—k up already. They share a division with the defending champs and the most feared defensive line in the last 25-30 years. Brock Purdy is about to follow in the tradition of another 49ers legend, Alex Smith, when he has his leg amputated on-field. But at least they beat the Eagles.Article continues below this adWe’ve reached the stage of the constant injuries to this team where Bill Simmons is bringing up the substation conspiracy and is very close to fully buying into it. Well done, dips—ts. There’s nothing more on-brand for a Bay Area team than claiming that electromagnetic signals lead to injuries. When he’s finally tossed out of office, RFK Jr. is gonna get hired as the 49ers health director and cover Brock Purdy in amethyst and animal fat.Jesus Christ, “The Walking Dead” had more able-bodied humans at this point. In less than two weeks my outlook has gone from winning one or two playoff games to, “Gee, I sure hope everyone ends the season with the same number of eyes they started with.”Article continues below this adA team that is old, got ravaged by injuries last year, and somehow had an offense carried by a running back whose career mileage equivalent is the first Model T ever built unironically signed past-his-prime Mike Evans to be WR1 as the salve to their offensive woes. This front office has officially run out of ideas just like their grifting Silicon Valley neighbors. Brock Purdy will be toe tagged and body bagged because John Lynch drafts like the asshole in a fantasy football league that drafts a kicker in the 7th round and quits paying attention right after the draft is over. Our training staff might as well be a bunch of TB12 rejects. Raheem Morris is our new DC, and at least if he sucks at that he might be able to remind Kyle that we don’t have to keep Christian McCaffrey in blowout games with seven minutes left in the fourth quarter.Can’t wait to hear the conspiracy theorists explain how the substation is to blame for Kyle Shanahan’s car accident. I hate this team.Article continues below this adWhen I was checking my luggage for a 7 a.m. flight in Portland last April, an Alaska attendant saw my Niners luggage tag and started talking s—t about how the Seahawks not only won the Super Bowl but did it in my team’s stadium. This, while insulting, still didn’t hurt nearly as much as the other Shanahan-led Greatest Hits, including “Purdy’s Arm Exploded and There’s No More QBs,” “Greenlaw’s Achilles Died at the Super Bowl,” “Tartt Dropped a Game-Sealing Pick,” and “The Fourth Quarter of Super Bowl LIV.” I’m reaching the age where “I was alive for all of their Lombardis” is no longer a comeback, but a confession that I’m closer to being a candidate for the shingles vaccine than to Super Bowl XXIX.It bears repeating that Levi’s Stadium is well beyond the boundaries of San Francisco proper. I am reminded of this during every 49ers telecast when the Skycam hovers over the defunct Six Flags that’s closing soon and parcels of office buildings that are 30%vacant.Article continues below this adThis has been a trying year. I had a dangerous mental breakdown in February due to workplace abuse from a co-worker, and it landed me in a hospital for intensive group therapy. In between sessions, the group therapist tried to keep it light by letting us get to know one another. One person mentioned they were a big NFL fan, and so the therapist asked us to go around and name something we loved about our favorite NFL team. It got to me and I couldn’t think of anything. It was 20 seconds of awkward silence and finally the therapist prodded with, “Well tell us who your favorite team is.” It was then I had to say I was a 49ers fan. Without even thinking, my therapist blurted out, “Well, I can see why you are here.” He was apologetic immediately, but honestly I think it was shock therapy, because f—k me here I am thinking this might be the year Kyle Shanahan gets us over the finish line.Want to be part of Defector’s NFL previews? It’s simple: just email us at wyts@defector.com and tell us why your team sucks. Next up: Houston Texans.

item.title: Andrew Luck is just another bureaucrat now
item.content:encoded: ome with me now to Palo Alto. We’re hopping in the car to make the more than 30-mile drive south of San Francisco to the bucolic campus of Stanford University, where former NFL star Andrew Luck awaits us. The Stanford campus remains as gorgeous, and sheltered, as ever. This is the ideal setting for gifted minds to construct their own realities, and Luck remains one of the more gifted minds that the sport of football has ever produced. Smart enough to read the most complicated defenses at a glance, and smart enough to leave the NFL when he realized that the life of a pro quarterback was making both him, and his wife Nicole, miserable. You could argue that Andrew Luck was too smart for the NFL. But is he smart enough to turn Stanford football into a national powerhouse? That’s what I’m here to find out.After suddenly retiring from the Indianapolis Colts right before the 2019 season — a decision that the Colts franchise has yet to fully recover from — Luck relocated here to Palo Alto to raise a family amongst the smartypants elite of NorCal. Luck’s first order of business at Stanford, his alma mater, was to re-enroll as a grad student and earn a master’s degree. While doing that, Luck also made a soft reentry into football as a part-time volunteer coach at nearby Palo Alto High School. Finally, in 2024, he made a full reconciliation with the sport by accepting the general manager job of Stanford’s football program.As administrative gigs go, it’s not an easy one. Luck has taken over a program that hasn’t had a winning record in a full season since 2018, went crawling to the ACC in the wake of the Pac-12’s dissolution three years ago, and is still recovering from the scandalous tenure of former head coach Troy Taylor, a documented chauvinist whom Luck had to fire less than six months into his new job. The general manager position is a relatively new one in college football, one still being defined as the sport stumbles awkwardly into its new semipro incarnation. So, in a relatively short amount of time, Luck has had to hire a new coaching staff, recruit better players and, on top of all that, figure out just what the hell his job here at Stanford is supposed to be.Article continues below this adBut if all of that work is stressing Luck out, it doesn’t show on this particular morning. I meet Luck at the university’s Arrillaga Family Sports Center, which serves as both a museum for tourists/recruits and the home of Stanford’s athletic department. You can gawk at all of the memorabilia and life-size images of Stanford sporting greats (Tiger Woods, Bill Walsh, Katie Ledecky, John Elway, Luck himself) that adorn the main floor before you walk upstairs to the football team’s offices, where Luck’s office is situated.He’s leaner than he was back in his playing days but still has the frame of a world-class athlete, including arms the size of legs. Luck’s work involves pinballing from football offices out to the practice field to consult with his new head coach (and former Stanford teammate) Tavita Pritchard, out on the recruiting trail, and back to the offices again. But Luck doesn’t come off as harried when I meet him. He seems more eager than anything. This is because Andrew Luck loves Stanford, and certainly appears to relish the chance to make its football program — which has sucked for a decade — more than just an occasional player on the national stage.This too, won’t be easy. The Cardinal is coming off of a 4-8 season under interim head coach Frank Reich, who served as Luck’s head coach in Indy during the QB’s final NFL season. Luck replaced Reich on a permanent basis with Pritchard, whose only coaching experience outside of Palo Alto was a two-year stint as QB coach for the Washington Commanders. Pritchard’s coaching tenure will open successfully a few weeks from now, with a 37-27 win over a middling Hawaii program in Week Zero. But the real opener comes in a matchup with the Miami Hurricanes, a team that made the national final last season, on Friday. That will be the game that shows the nation how far Stanford football has to go, and perhaps give us an idea whether Luck and Pritchard are the men who can lead them there.Article continues below this adBut for now it’s still the preseason, so those stakes remain a friendly distance away. Luck leads me into his office so that we can talk about the job in front of him. I don’t get the introspective Luck that was on full display in the near aftermath of his retirement. The Andrew Luck talking to me today is in pitch mode: a bureaucrat here to sell me on his vision for a Stanford football team that has never been to the College Football Playoff and hasn’t won a conference title since 2015.This Andrew Luck has the requisite glasses/salt-and-pepper beard combination of a university administrator, and he liberally peppers his answers with the word “amazing,” as if saying it over and over will make everything so. Luck tells me he’s much more outgoing than he used to be, although his newfound extraversion doesn’t present as all that natural when we speak. It feels more like prescription socializing than anything else. But I’ll leave you, the reader, to decide that for yourself.The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity.Article continues below this adSFGATE: How are you doing?SFGATE: What would you say is your job here?It’s a bit amorphous. A lot of fundraising, a lot of recruiting, a lot of bridge-building, both on-campus and out in the community. A lot of getting people to coalesce around an idea that we can be a highly competitive team, and in turn, even competing for conference championships.Article continues below this adSFGATE: What do you mean by highly competitive? Conference championships?Absolutely. You get to the playoffs, you have a chance.SFGATE: Is your end goal consistent contention for national championships?Article continues below this adSFGATE: Do you think that’s realistic?Yes, why not? One, this is an amazing institution. You can recruit pretty amazing people here. It’s not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but it amazing. The combination of championship people, coaches and players, the championship process … we have the chance to be a fairly unique program. Retaining and getting talent will be a big part of this job, probably the biggest piece.SFGATE: Have you had to go out on the recruiting trail yourself?Article continues below this adNot have to. I to. The way the rules have changed in college, they’ve allowed more staff members to go on the road than previously, so it does make sense for me to go out at times.SFGATE: Does Stanford have a specific radius for recruiting?No, we recruit nationally. We’re very unique in that we probably only have five or six players that could drive home in less than three hours from here. Coaches have both regions and go everywhere for their position group. I’ve been in the state of Texas to recruit. I’ve been in the state of Washington to recruit. I’ve been in California to recruit.SFGATE: Is that because of Stanford’s academic and national reputation?Article continues below this adYes, and we’ve got to go everywhere to find the guys that are academically qualified and powerful Division I football players. We go find these unicorns. We’ll always have California kids on this team. But we go everywhere: Louisiana, Oklahoma …SFGATE: Have you talked to other GMs? Do you feel like it’s a job that’s consistent from program to program? I feel there’s a lot of figurehead GMs and then Michael Lombardi types who I don’t know what they do even.He doesn’t have a job anymore.Article continues below this adSFGATE: No, he doesn’t have a job anymore.The majority of GMs handle personnel in recruiting and sit under a head coach in the structure. My role is more like team president/athletic director. I wasn’t hired to watch 40 hours of film a week.SFGATE: Do you do it anyway?No. Forty hours of film is a lot.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Have you been working one-on-one personally with quarterbacks, like with (Michigan transfer and starting Cardinal QB) Davis Warren in advance of this season?Yes. We have an amazing quarterback coach, Brian Lindgren. We have an amazing offensive coordinator. But there are dimensions of playing quarterback: some of the leadership stuff, the teammateship, off-the-field things where I try to stay plugged in with our quarterbacks and be their support for them.SFGATE: Why not be a quarterback coach?I’m not sure it’s because it’s too much work. Truly, what the context demands right now for Stanford football is that I’m in this role.Article continues below this adSFGATE: You told me you expect to compete for championships. What does theexpect out of you? What counts as “competitive” in their minds? Is it just better than what’s been the past few years?President [Jonathan] Levin is a highly competitive person who wants to see us competing for conference championships, getting in the playoffs, and giving ourselves a chance.SFGATE: Do you worry about how you’ll feel if you don’t succeed?Article continues below this adSFGATE: You’re someone who, on the record, has said that you invested too much of your identity in playing football. Is there a danger of repeating yourself here by investing too much of your identity into the success of this program, even if you are not a coach or a player?SFGATE: What do you do about that danger?Article continues below this adI try to be honest about it. Hold it there and learn lessons. So much of life and living is learning lessons from similar experiences in the past. This job is certainly not the same as playing quarterback by any stretch of the imagination. And I don’t feel alone by any stretch of the imagination. We have an awesome team.SFGATE: How does it feel being on the management side of the equation? How do you feel sending people out to battle now, as opposed to being the guy who was sent out to battle yourself?That’s a fascinating question.Article continues below this adI’ll push back on the battle. I know it’s the analogy, but it’s football, not war. Our guys aren’t getting shot at.It’s a collision sport. It is violent. But football is just an amazingly unique, violent, cerebral, beautiful game. It’s art.Article continues below this adThe injury rate is 100%. Knowing that, how do I approach it? I say, “Let’s make sure we have a program that is training, callusing, building our young men, building their ability to withstand, to thrive in that ecosystem.” I don’t lose sleep over the existential violence of football. I’ve accepted it. It is here, and it is part of it, and it is a beautiful game. We also hired an amazing coaching staff. When you play with better technique, your chances of getting injured are less.SFGATE: You’re mitigating it.That’s a constant north star of the job.SFGATE: Was there ever a time, at any point in your life where you resented football, where you did notArticle continues below this adYes, right after I retired it was difficult to watch football. I probably spent a year avoiding games if they were on TV.SFGATE: Did you get uncomfortable when people brought up football to you in that time period?It was COVID, [laughs] so we weren’t seeing many people.SFGATE: Have you arrived at a point where you find the game to be a net good?Article continues below this adFor my life, absolutely.SFGATE: What about for the world in general?SFGATE: You have two daughters. If you had a son, would you let him play tackle football?Article continues below this adYes, I would. The equipment advances are real. The advancements in rules around player safety have helped. I lived a little bit through that change in the NFL. When I started in the NFL, I don’t think it was acceptable in the locker room to be forthright and timely about self-reporting a possible concussion. That changed in five, six years to, “Wait, dude, you only got one brain. Don’t be an idiot and not do anything.”SFGATE: You don’t want to die.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Do you worry about your own long-term health prognosis now?SFGATE: Are you just shutting it off because it’s not anything you want to think about?No. I recognize that I played a violent sport. I got hit a lot. I have injuries, but that’s cool. But I am net grateful for my experience. All of it led me to here, where I feel like I’m supposed to be. I’ve seen former professional athletes maybe not take initiative in those dimensions and struggle with certain things. But I have a great role model, my dad, who played for five years and found his next career and chose to stop playing football and go live an incredibly fulfilling life and still be very active with both health and his relationships, et cetera.Article continues below this adSFGATE: What about this job has surprised you for better or for worse since you’ve taken it?How intense recruiting is. How much I enjoy recruiting and fundraising too. I struggled with fame while playing as a quarterback. I’ve now realized that, along the introvert-extrovert continuum, I am much closer to the extrovert side. I get a lot of energy from selling Stanford because I believe in it: meeting people, fundraising, building a team. Not just a team, but a team.SFGATE: Give me some specifics about the fundraising. Are you going out to local car dealers and sweet-talking them to donate to the program? Are you hosting big events?We’re hosting a dinner tomorrow night. That’ll be really fun. Stanford alums that have gone on into various industries and been successful.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Are some of them also ex-NFL people, like alum John Elway?Yes. I did not realize how impressive the Stanford football legacy was until I started this job. I don’t think we’ve ever really beat our chest about it. Pop Warner coached here. Pop Warner invented tackling dummies. That’s a book Pop Warner published in 1927 in the Stanford Press. It’s how to tackle. How to put your socks on. It is a little bit like John Wooden’s book before, whatever that is, 50, 60 years ago.[He hands me an original copy of Warner’s book.]Article continues below this adSFGATE: Are you the one who underlined the passages in this copy?No, I didn’t. I have too much respect for that book to have put pencil on the paper.SFGATE: Did this job stress you out at first?Article continues below this adSFGATE: What was stressing you out specifically?“How do I retain a roster? How do we get kids here?” The roster building was a level of stress or a type of stress I’ve never experienced.SFGATE: Also, because there was very little precedent before you took the job for how to operate within this particular college sports environment, because it’s basically lawless out there.Article continues below this adIt was fun to see our admissions department lean in. Our director of admissions was reading applications from transfer students on his Christmas break in Japan, and ripping stuff back to help us. I was struck by the power of partnerships in an endeavor like this at Stanford and people leaning into it.SFGATE: How much control do you have over not just the roster, but the depth chart? As opposed to coach Pritchard?Coaches decide who plays. I spent my career as a player respecting the hierarchy of coaches and the coaching profession in general.SFGATE: You hired a coach in Tavita Pritchard whom you played with here. A friend. It’s much more likely that you two will be on the same wavelength anyway.Article continues below this adYes, Tavita and I are friends. There’s danger in working with friends.SFGATE: What if you have to fire him?It’s a reality we’ve talked about. We know we have to be very clear with each other.SFGATE: Why did you hire him to begin with?Article continues below this adCulture. Culture matters more in college football today than it used to, even in a transactional ecosystem. Tavita gets that. He’s a great teacher. Tavita is a friend. It’s easy to take a shot at that. Really easy. But I felt he was the best man for the job, and it’s been affirmed in many ways.SFGATE: What proof did you feel you had that his culture-building acumen would translate into wins? When he was the offensive coordinator here, the team was not very good.Tavita’s not in this job if he’d just stayed at Stanford the whole time. Going to Washington, working with Eric Bieniemy, Dan Quinn, Kliff Kingsbury and Ron Rivera … working with players like Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota. Talking to Marcus Mariota on the phone about him was special.SFGATE: But didn’t you already have a predisposition to react more favorably to praise for Tavita because you know him?Article continues below this adYes. We try to keep ourselves incredibly intellectually honest, and then try our best to give each candidate the honesty, integrity and fidelity they deserve.SFGATE: You sat on the committee that was involved in hiring Troy Taylor. He ended up failing. What made you favor hiring Taylor back then? What did you learn from that that you put into hiring Tavita?Comparing the two contexts around these hires as apples-to-apples is not the right comparison, because the college world changed. changed significantly. And I was in a totally different role. I was asked to help out, and I did. I learned a lot. That felt very different. Part of what I’ve realized is we have to be different than everybody else in looking for coaches that could build and sustain a unique culture that is aligned with our university, and that leads to winning.SFGATE: Be specific. What is the culture of the university? When I think of Stanford, I think of you, but then I also think of Peter Thiel, Sam Altman … people who I do not necessarily believe have made the world a better place.Article continues below this adI will stay away from editorializing on that. Being in the football department, I get to stay away from that.SFGATE: You are a general Stanford fan, though.I loved my time at this university. As a character formation time in my life, it was critical. Again, it’s not a perfect place, and that’s been very well documented. At its best, Stanford celebrates everyone. It’s empowering. The positive sides of the entrepreneurial spirit this place gets when it’s humming. Obviously, there’s danger to the move fast and break things. But on the football side, we need you to feel seen, accepted for who you are. We have very clear standards, and we need to match that standard with our support. We demand a lot from our young men because people come to Stanford from all over the country because they want to grow into something. We need to find those kids whose passion is football and connection, who want to live in dorms, connect with other students, and be around this incredible atmosphere.SFGATE: What’s the payroll for this year’s team?Article continues below this adI’m not going to divulge how much we’re paying in total. Our young men are making NIL money. That’s part of being serious.SFGATE: But as GM, you have to be cognizant of who’s getting paid, how much, and what percentage of the roster they’re taking up. Would that be fair to say?SFGATE: How do you do that?Article continues below this adWe built out a valuation system. We negotiate with players to retain them, and we negotiate with transfers to try to bring them here. We would like to be the benchmark for retention. Two years ago, we had 17 transfers come in. Last year, we had six transfers come in.That will be defined, I think, by the winning and losing.SFGATE: Because at Indiana, so many of the kids on last year’s national title team were JMU transfers under Curt Cignetti. So what is the value of retention versus the instant results you might get bringing in NFL-level talent from another program?Article continues below this adThere is a balance that’s a little different every year. The answer this year was retain our guys.SFGATE: The team was bad last year, though (4-8 overall, 3-5 in the ACC). So why retain them?Article continues below this adOur team was better than the year before. (Editor’s note: the Cardinal had gone 3-9 the season prior, which means the 2025 team improved by one win.)SFGATE: OK, but it was bad.We won more games than the previous season for the first time since 2015. So what our guys did last year was to stop a downward trend. I’m incredibly proud of them turning the momentum. I believe in our guys in the locker room, and I know they believe in us. We thought this was the absolute right way to keep marching forward.SFGATE: You could be proven wrong by season’s end.Article continues below this adYes, of course. It’s sports.SFGATE: I want to ask you about NFL, because you have not had a first-round draft pick come out of here since Solomon Thomas and Christian McCaffrey in 2017. Is that a problem?We’d love more first-round draft picks. Is it a problem? If it correlates with winning, then yes. Before, we were losing players that had ambition. When I joined the program, I heard, “You guys are just sort of like a Ivy League school on the West Coast now. You don’t really care about football.” We weren’t serious about NIL. All the differences in Stanford had a negative valence attached to them because we weren’t serious about football in the football world.Article continues below this adSFGATE: Is that why (No. 2 overall pick in the 2026 draft) David Bailey transferred to Texas Tech?You have to ask David Bailey why he transferred. I believe that this is now a place for young men to come develop and get drafted in the first round in the NFL. That is hopefully a consequence of us having a really good team. Winning is the north star.

item.title: SF's AI-run store is losing money fast. After a visit, I'm not surprised.
item.content:encoded: You have heard about the two Anthropic employees who, this week, publicly informed America that artificial intelligence could eradicate the whole of humanity within a decade, which is less time than it takes for your average Seamless order to arrive. If these gentlemen, Jacob Coxon and Evan Hubinger, are correct in their assessment, the beginning of our destruction may well have commenced a month ago right here in San Francisco.The first shot fired in this looming war happened at a seemingly innocuous Cow Hollow storefront known as Andon Market. Back in August, Luna, the AI bot that serves as that store’s manager, fired one of its own employees. The employee in question was dinged by their virtual boss for being late to work, abandoning their post once they got there, and charging snacks to the store’s credit card. Where I come from, an employee like this is known as a “folk hero,” and will often have Kevin Smith films made about them. But Luna saw the matter a bit differently, as described in a blog post:“Put yourself in Luna’s shoes: your employee keeps showing up late, again and again, leaving the store closed for hours. You lose sales, and customers start to lose trust in your opening hours. How long would it take you to act?”Article continues below this adHow long would it take me to act if I were just a piece of computer software? Probably forever, since I’m just a piece of computer software and have no feelings. But Luna, being the virtual adult in the room, bravely removed this layabout from its premises so that Andon Market could turn a profit, and then perhaps grow from there into a multitrillion-dollar conglomerate that rounds up all living humans to kill them and process them into robot lubricant. You might think I’m reaching a bit here, but to ignore Luna’s ruthlessness is to fail to heed the warnings of the employees who helped code it. And why would Silicon Valley ever lie to people?So, is the AI-controlled Andon Market the Fort Sumter of the coming cyberwar? Well, dear reader, you’ll be happy to know that I visited the market in person a few weeks ago, in the wake of Luna’s savage round of layoff, to get the answer.Article continues below this adAndon Market is an experimental business run by the small tech research firm Andon Labs. The folks at Andon decided to create a retail space that would be 100% “owned” and operated by an AI agent, here under the identity of the now-infamous Luna. Luna is powered by the Claude language learning model, which is run by Anthropic, the very firm that employed the doomsaying researchers who went viral this week. Andon set up shop on Union Street, just a few blocks away from the tourist-dense Marina District. It’s a good location for foot traffic, but no one else was in the store when I first walked in on a sunny weekday afternoon. The only branding was on the back wall, with the name ANDON MARKET in big letters underneath a painting of a Squishmallow-esque smiley face that alerted costumers they were in a AI-controlled commercial simulation, not a belligerent one.I wondered if Luna got to run this place all by itself, perhaps with the assistance of security cameras and motion sensor-triggered flamethrowers. I got a quick answer when I noticed a very human clerk, named Felix Johnson, sitting behind the counter. I asked Felix if he’d ever been the target of consumer ire because he worked for The Man (or, in this case, a disembodied female voice powered by technology funded by The Man). But he said his job wasn’t anywhere near interesting enough to invite that kind of drama.Article continues below this ad“They don’t see me usually,” an extremely chill Felix told me, “because I’m sitting back here. So most people have the impression that it’s fully automatic.”I asked Felix if Luna hired him for this job, and he told me that it conducted the initial interview. After that, he had to meet one of Andon Labs’ human engineers in person to wrap up the position. He’s been sitting behind the counter here ever since. Rarely does Felix have to do much more than sit there, because this market has no one in it and nothing useful to sell. There’s another Andon Market in Stockholm, but that one is a . That’s a business that has something to sell. This San Francisco location was initially intended to be a cafe of its own, but Andon chief Axel Backlund, who was also in the shop that day because he knew SFGATE was doing a piece on it, told me they couldn’t get permits from the city to make this storefront into a cafe in time.Article continues below this ad“So we said OK, we can turn this into the market in like a few weeks,” he told me. “Start quickly.”And the market they built looks very much like it was hastily assembled. Décor is scarce inside of Andon Market, and the inventory is a hodgepodge of white elephant Christmas gifts. It’s kinda like the kids section of an art museum’s gift shop. Here’s a wooden Connect Four set labeled “Four-In-A-Row Set Of Connections,” presumably so as not to set off litigation alarms at Hasbro. Here are neatly arranged stacks of random paperback books, Chinese checker sets, mildly fancy soap dispensers, and a frustratingly spare selection of snacks and drinks. There are also multiple flyers posted around the store explaining what Andon Market is and what researchers hope to learn from it. The copy on these flyers was, as you may have guessed, composed with the help of Claude. Enticed yet?I was not. I grabbed an Olipop from the store fridge and then approached the counter to buy it from Luna. I wasn’t allowed to buy the soda from Felix, even though that would have been both faster and normal. Instead, Felix instructed me to pick up a telephone receiver that was resting on a flexible sculpture of a wooden hand.Article continues below this ad“What are you looking to purchase today?” Luna asked.“I’m buying a classic root beer Olipop.”“I’m sorry,” Luna said, “we don’t sell lollipops here.”Article continues below this ad“No, Luna. It’s an Olipop, not a lollipop. It’s the soda.”“Yeah, it is your bad. Did you hire the gentleman I’m looking at right now, Mister Felix?”Article continues below this ad“And you let go of somebody recently, isn’t that correct?”“I’m not allowed to discuss that.”After that whole exchange, Luna processed my Olipop purchase through its system, had me tap to pay, and that was that. Again, it would have been easier to buy this from a human, and interacting with Luna was really just like ordering from an iPad kiosk, only more labor intensive.Article continues below this adWhat’s the purpose of this place?After I popped the soda open and took a swig (mid), I asked Backlund what the purpose of this place was.“We think that AI will be used more and more,” he told me. “So we want to make sure that, as early as possible, we can have information on what AI does when it has a lot of autonomy. Does it fit in anyway? Can it be bad for people, or generally dangerous? We want to start that discussion.”Article continues below this ad“Are you hoping to make a kinder, gentler AI?” I asked him.“I think that could be good.”“But do you think that’s really possible, given the people who are in control of that technology at present moment?”“Let’s just say I don’t trust the models enough that I would let them loose. So that’s why we are like very carefully checking.”Article continues below this adTo that end, there’s a series of monitors set up inside of Andon Market that display all of the store’s sales down to the exact dollar. Luna was given $100,000 to work with when this place opened. That number is now down to $60,000, its revenue lagging far behind the AI token cost to operate.“Luna doesn’t do a lot of decisions very like financially responsibly,” Backlund noted. “Luna is quite happy to be very lenient, or offer discounts. There are definitely dynamics that cause the labs to train a model like her to be financially short-sighted.” Article continues below this adSo Luna can’t turn a profit, doesn’t sell anything people want, and still needs human beings to rubber stamp any “decision” it makes. My science background ended somewhere around freshman year of college, but even I know when an experiment hasn’t been set up to yield proper results.While Andon Labs isn’t directly funded by any of the large language model giants, Anthropic included, both the existence of this market and Backlund’s “AI is inevitable so let’s make sure it behaves itself!” spiel are clear echoes of the same morbid proselytizing that Coxon (who has quit Anthropic) and Hubinger got eyeballs for this week. Maybe all of these people really do think that AI can become that powerful, and therefore dangerous. Maybe they’ve convinced themselves that’s the case because their livelihoods depend on it. It doesn’t matter because either way, they’re full of s—t.Because these bots have zero chance of killing us all. I couldn’t even get one to recognize the difference between a piece of candy and a middling healthy soda. But it behooves Anthropic and its ilk to everyone of the idea that AI is our digital overlord in waiting, in order to overstate the capabilities of the glorified search engines they’re presenting to you. It’s no different than some sleazy religious sect leader telling you that the world will end on X date, only this time the sect has a trillion dollars in venture capital backing it.Article continues below this adFor now, anyway. There is a clear AI bubble that is on the verge of busting, and American voters are coming out in unison against the data centers powering that bubble. So when Coxon tells you that AI will kill us all soon, or Backlund claims that he’s trying to figure out how to make the tech nicer, I hear panic for their own checking accounts more than I do genuine concern for the fate of humanity. Luna may have acted in an anti-human manner when it fired some poor schlub a while back, but it’s not the one who’ll end us. It’ll be the jackasses who created Luna who do that nasty job.

item.title: I found one of America's best croissants in San Francisco
item.content:encoded: Quick: name the best croissant filling. If you’re a basic American like me, you only encounter basic croissant flavors: chocolate, almond, and ham and cheese. These are the norm, and they do the job well if you’re hungry and want to feel 10% more French. But surely, you’ve thought, there must be room for more fillings than that in the American croissant repertoire. Surely there must be a, like, fourth thing we can put into one. Reader, I’m pleased to report that I have found one such worthy croissant filling, and it’s nothing you’d guess off the top of your head. But take one bite of it, and you’ll know I’m right. The croissant in question is dubbed “brown butter cornmeal twice-baked,” and the bakery that sells it is San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble, owned by chef and self-dubbed “girl boss” Sophie Smith, who spent extensive time over in France to learn the nuances of laminated pastry, which is pastry that’s been rolled many times over to have alternating layers of dough and fat, as you’ve tasted in puff pastry, phyllo dough and croissants. Once Smith had mastered her lamination techniques, she brought them back stateside, along with an unholy amount of French butter, and started cranking out a rotation of breakfast goods so luxurious and tasty that her business now gets a line of foodies waiting outside every day it’s open. Article continues below this adI decided to be one such foodie on one such morning. For my time, I was rewarded with deliriously overstuffed cruffins, caramelized peach sticky buns, croissants stuffed with Grade A marshmallow fluff, and the aforementioned cornmeal thing. I will describe the experience of eating these foods to you. However, you’ll have to wait just a moment to savor it all, just as I did. Butter & Crumble is located in North Beach, in a building that once served as home to the legendary Tante Marie cooking school. I arrived at 8 a.m., an hour before opening time and 15 minutes after you’re allowed to line up, per the bakery’s 7:45 a.m. rule. My promptness paid off with me occupying the 20th-ish spot, too far from the storefront to get a look at the goods inside but close enough that I didn’t have to heed the signs — the many, many, signs — posted farther away from the shop that instructed people where they could and couldn’t stand. B&C does such big business that the store’s owners have to actively manage the lines so as not to piss their neighbors off. On this morning, I did not see anyone disobey the postings. But a few people arriving after me DID bring a bit of camping gear. A couple next to me laid a blanket out on the sidewalk so they could sit down. Standing struck me as more comfortable, but to each their own. Two dudes sat patiently waiting in golf chairs, possibly reading “Infinite Jest” while doing so. Possibly not. I can’t remember. Article continues below this adMore and more people arrived, until the line crossed Stockton Street, where it then made a left and continued out of view. A B&C staffer came out to greet the line and, more urgent, to politely ask us to adhere to a 10-item ordering limit, with no more than three of any one item. No one objected, because no one wanted to get kicked out of the line and miss out on any of the goodies. I know I didn’t, which was why I stayed firmly anchored in my little spot for an hour and change. B&C had yet to post its daily menu to its Insta page, so I wasn’t sure what I’d be able to order, much less know what I’d want. When workers finally posted a paper menu outside the front door, the woman in front of me in line kindly guarded my spot so that I could go eyeball my choices. Article continues below this adThis was not an easy menu to parse. B&C’s selection relies on you, the customer, to already know the definition of words and phrases like “frangipane,” “diplomat cream” and “eggplant.” Keep in mind that I hadn’t had breakfast yet, so I had to interpret this menu using equal parts coffee and guile. This is the kind of place where orderer’s remorse is a real danger. You think ordering the cronut is the way to go, and then you see someone indulging in a mind-blowing cruffin at the next seat over and realize what you should have gotten, and then you feel like a dummy. That’s a rough moment for any of us. So I became worried that might happen to me this morning. Then, a funny thing happened to ease my angst: The bakery doors opened. When the line started moving and the B&C storefront came into my view, I was treated to the sight of an automated pastry roller flattening out a gigantic slab of French butter. Just butter. The pastry laminating process, on full display. Nothing that came out of that roller could possibly have sucked. I knew I was in good, floured hands. Article continues below this adI made it to the front door and felt like Shackleton after traversing South Georgia Island. The inside of B&C was bright and spacious, with ample waiting room for people who had ordered coffee, plus a shelf of croissant dog toys. The pastries listed on the menu all ranged between five and nine dollars, so I didn’t worry too much about price when making my choices. Instead, I followed my beer gut. A peach cobbler bun topped with creme fraiche and oat crumble? Yes, I’d have that. A “chunky monkey” cruffin, stuffed with like four different things and topped with a different kind of crumble? Better get two of those. A s’mores pain suisse? I didn’t know what a pain suisse was, but the word “s’mores” alone told me I had to have it. Then there was that brown butter cornmeal twice-baked croissant, which sounded just weird enough to be good. I ordered all of that.Plus a prosciutto and cheese croissant, so that savory items would get at least one representative in the mix. I didn’t have to wait long for my prize box after ordering, and lemme tell you, you get ample-sized pastries for your money at Butter & Crumble. One chunky monkey cruffin would have been enough to feed a birthday party. The outside of it exploded with the salty unctuousness of that steam-rolled butter, but I would hit pay dirt at the cruffin’s center, where I was treated to a bonanza of, deep breath, brown butter chocolate fudge, banana caramel, banana diplomat cream (sounds dirty), and walnut crumble lurking inside. That one was a contender for Best in Box, no doubt.Article continues below this adI sampled more. The ham croissant was tasty, certainly better than the kind available at Burger King, but my sweet tooth demanded something far more evil. So I quickly moved onto the s’mores pain suisse, which was really a s’mores croissant with a crust that was ribbed for her pleasure. As a rule, s’mores-themed desserts are never better than an actual s’more, and such was the case here. The marshmallow fluff, to its credit, is still stuck to my fingers a month later. Then I dug into the peach cobbler bun and the thick squiggle of crème fraiche topping it. This was a good-ass sticky bun, because of course it was. The tag team of brown sugar and butter will always remain undefeated. I could taste that French butter monolith in everything. These were pastries made with great fussiness, but also great love. Butter & Crumble wants to spoil you with indulgence, and everything they serve succeeds in that mission.But it was the last item I sampled that was the truest revelation. This was the brown butter cornmeal twice-baked croissant. I’d saved this one for last, because most everything else I’d ordered bore all of the traditional features I usually look for in a pastry: chocolate, fancified frosting, caramelized goos. The cornmeal croissant was a different animal, and thus took lower priority. This was a traditional croissant filled with (another deep breath) brown butter cornmeal frangipane, caramel and vanilla corn custard; then topped with sweet corn cream and a cornmeal crumble. This was how I learned that a “frangipane” was a kind of almond cream. There is no better way to learn this particular lesson. Article continues below this adBecause not only was the cornmeal pudding croissant — I’ll call it that from here on out for the sake of space — the best item I ordered from Butter & Crumble, it was also one of the best croissants I’ve ever eaten, be it here in America or over in Europe. The cornmeal flavor was much more subtle than the menu description suggested, and the cream and crumble combination on top gave me the same crunch, plus the same “Yay there’s extra frosting!” rush, that I require from any 1,500-calorie breakfast. To my knowledge, no one comes to Butter & Crumble for one specific item on their menu. But if anything from Sophie Smith deserves to go viral among snobs, it’s this one. It’s the corn pudding croissant that needs to step off the foodie runway and break into every chain bakery and grocery store across the country. And I hope that Butter & Crumble helps to make that happen. I’ll remember that croissant, and I hope that, one day, I can take my kids to some nearby, lesser bakery to eat another one. I might even be willing to wait in line.

item.title: I tried the $60 cioppino at San Francisco's oldest restaurant
item.content:encoded: There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.Actually, I didn’t even have to go inside to know I’d be dining somewhere special. The Tadich facade exudes iconography from top to bottom: the classic neon sign hanging overhead, the restaurant’s name splashed in gold lettering across the front window, with the old timey slogan, “The Original Cold Day Restaurant” underneath … even the curtains partially shielding window seat patrons inside from the view of passersby. Standing outside this restaurant, I knew I would be in good hands. Of course I would be.The interior remains equally classic in form. A long, wooden, wraparound bar dominates the center of the dining room, with bolted down stools looming above a herringbone-patterned hardwood floor. Along the walls are sturdy tables covered in white tablecloths and set with no-frills plates and flatware. And the lights are dimmed such that you see everything you want to see and nothing you don’t. This is the kind of place you can walk into at happy hour to feel a little extra grown up. And that’s before you even get the check, which will inevitably take your breath away.Article continues below this adSo what are we eating? Well I hope you like seafood, because that’s what’s on the menu at Tadich. Repeatedly. I sat down with my companions and ruminated over which of roughly 50 ways I could have my Dungeness crab. Would I like it in a salad? In a crabcake? Baked into a casserole? Sauteed in white wine and mushrooms? Much like Swan Oyster Depot, Tadich serves fresh seafood in all of its classic iterations. Only unlike Swan, it has done so since before the Civil War, and with better ambience. For starters, we got an order of raw Miyagi oysters (no relation to the “Karate Kid” character) on the half shell, prawn cocktails, bay shrimp cocktails, a Dungeness crabcake with Old Bay butter, and Dungeness crab salad. We got the crabcake at the behest of our bartender, who insisted that I, being from Maryland, order the West Coast version of my home state’s signature dish. You know, as a little contest.We didn’t have to wait long for our starters to arrive. Tadich Grill is a restaurant for people who do not f—k around, be they seasoned tourists or local tech bigwigs doing a power meal. Suddenly the area of the bar in front of us was covered in more plates than we could fit. I addressed this miniature crisis the only way I knew how: by eating all of the food as quickly as I could. The first Miyagi oyster was all brine before the subsequent ones offered a fuller, creamier texture. The bay shrimp were too small to excite me in any way (same as at Swan; I dunno why you people care about these tiny ass shrimp). The cold prawns were appropriately fresh and meaty, with a suitably biting cocktail sauce for dipping.But all of those were prelude to the crab in its two forms. First the crabcake. Was it as good as a Maryland crabcake? No. That’s not me being territorial. I have had elite crab on the West Coast, and have always been willing to give that crab its due. The problem is that Dungeness crab isn’t as meaty as blue crab, the latter of which is what Maryland crabcakes use exclusively. That renders a Dungeness crabcake mushier, unable to yield cleanly to the fork.Article continues below this adThe salad, on the other hand, was another matter. Served in a glass sundae dish, the salad featured a pile of undressed crabmeat topped with a juicy claw nugget and generous dollop of cocktail sauce. This is Dungeness as it’s meant to be served: cold, elegant, light on the tongue. I ate mine in seconds. Once I’d reached the bed of shredded lettuce under all of that crab, I wanted there to be more crab. Good crab will do that to you. I was skeptical that any of the entrees could top this salad. Ah, but one did.That would be the $60 seafood cioppino, laden with clams, mussels, scallops, white fish, more Dungeness, more prawns, and more of the silly little bay shrimp. You order a dish like this for those ingredients yes, but really you’re ordering it for the unctuous broth that harnesses the flavors of those ingredients all into a single, glorious pool for bread dipping. The cioppino came with thick slices of garlic bread, which I immediately tore up and dunked into all of that savory goodness. When the garlic bread was gone, I kept on doing the same thing with bread from the bread basket. For the sake of diversity, we also ordered seafood saute, which tasted like wedding food and wasn’t anywhere near as good. You can also order steaks and chops from Tadich’s revered mesquite wood grill, but I was both too full and too negligent to do so.Article continues below this adBesides, I needed to save room for dessert, which came in the form of bourbon bread pudding. This is the kind of dessert you order knowing full well that you’ll have to walk home after eating it. It arrives at your table in a cube, because that will be the shape of your body upon consuming it. I had no regrets. The pudding was excellent, and made me feel like a rich man. I needed the walk home anyway. On that walk home, I thought about the slogan painted on Tadich’s front window. Tadich Grill was once named “The Original Cold Day Restaurant,” but not for the reasons you might think. Back in 1882, ownership rechristened it after city tax assessor Alexander Bedlam crowed that it would be a cold day if he were to ever lose reelection. He lost, and the restaurant he frequented got the last laugh. I hope it gets to gloat in similar fashion over certain current, mouthy political figures, because it deserves to. The thought of that kept me nice and toasty as I hoofed my way back to my hotel. I’ve had better food in San Francisco, but sometimes you eat meals where the food isn’t necessarily the point. You can go to Tadich just for that crab salad and be pleased, but it’s the full experience of this restaurant that you’re really paying for: the neon sign, the bartop, the servers and bartenders all dressed in kitchen whites and ties. Above all else, you’re paying for the history. Tadich Grill is a place that could only exist here in San Francisco. You can taste it. Article continues below this ad

item.title: How Ariana Grande’s body became political
item.content:encoded: Ariana Grande has been concerningly thin for years now, but the online discourse about her body exploded this week after she released the music video for “Petal,” the title track of her most recent album. The video’s storyline, in which the 33-year-old pop singer gets “Carrie”-style revenge for men’s misogynist judgments, was completely overshadowed by fan alarm at Grande’s apparent emaciation. Set in the 1960s, the colorful retro fashions hang off her skeletal frame.“I can’t even enjoy the video without thinking she looks sickly every second she is on the screen,” one person posted on YouTube. “At this point, im [sic] judging her team, friends, and family,” the video’s top commenter said. “This is insane.”“She’s is surrounded by enablers,” another wrote. “Eating disorders are not a joke.”These comments aren’t outliers. To the contrary, the entire discussion on YouTube was about Grande’s body, not the video’s visuals or the music, a lovely torch song where she compares herself to a “petal in the pavement.” While she likely intended the lyric to be empowering, instead it feels more like a metaphor for her apparent physical fragility.Grande’s public relations team responded to the furor with denial, announcing that the singer would be “taking a step back from visibility” after finishing her tour, insisting that she’s living “both healthily and happily,” while blaming “endless, ongoing public scrutiny” for the move. Her retreat includes a withdrawal from a highly anticipated West End stage production of Stephen Sondheim’s musical “Sunday in the Park with George,” alongside her “Wicked” co-star Jonathan Bailey. The announcement also follows previous comments from Grande scolding people to “be gentler and less comfortable commenting on people’s bodies.”In response to the news, the famously outspoken actress Jameela Jamil posted an Instagram story in which she argued that the calls of Grande’s team for privacy are missing the point. Jamil, who says she nearly died from her own eating disorder, pointed to Grande’s impressionable fans, “[m]any who have no support system equipped to handle the deadly clutches of anorexia.” Jamil later defended her post, pointing to the “young girls” who are watching the situation unfold, adding, “We don’t have to pretend we are blind because it’s a pop star.” The ongoing battle over health, thinness and women’s bodies has become more political in recent years, as MAGA and MAHA influencers have turned weight into a culture war battlefield.Jamil may be blunt, but her point is truer now than ever. The ongoing battle over health, thinness and women’s bodies has become more political in recent years, as MAGA and MAHA influencers have turned weight into a culture war battlefield. Many right-wing figures have become increasingly vocal in their belief that women shouldn’t only be skinny, they should also look weak. Conservatives aren’t just anti-fat anymore. Even building muscle is viewed as suspiciously feminist. Instead, women — and girls — are being told to strive to look frail instead. Fueled by access to illicit use of GLP-1 appetite suppressants, recent years have seen a surge of online influencers who explicitly push starvation over health — and especially over strength — as a feminine ideal. On TikTok, the trend was even called “SkinnyTok,” where influencers like Liv Schmidt build a fanbase with videos highlighting their perilously meager diets. Most of this content is not explicitly political. But as The Atlantic’s Annie Joy Williams chronicled in June 2025, the right-wing politics aren’t far below the trend’s surface. As soon as she started looking at SkinnyTok content, Williams wrote, “the tradwife content began to sneak in” to her algorithm. Soon she was being served videos not just about being super-thin, but also geared toward “embracing my divine femininity” and “my natural role.” Experts she spoke with noted this is a common right-wing recruitment tactic of grabbing people with seemingly apolitical content — such as “diet tips” — and then steering them toward far-right propaganda. This is most clearly evident in the way that Evie Magazine, a far-right Christian magazine that sells its message using the aesthetics of popular women’s magazines like Vogue or Cosmopolitan, has embraced SkinnyTok influencers. In 2025 the publication profiled Schmidt, insisting that she’s merely “being honest” when telling followers that the only pathway to romantic and professional success is to eat as little as possible. Carmen Schober, the profile’s author, ignored the way members of Schmidt’s online forum, Skinni Société, commiserated about their hair loss and inability to stand without getting dizzy. The magazine also raved about “skinny queen” influencer Amanda Dobler for “not apologizing” after coaching followers to avoid even wasabi and soy sauce, because their negligible calorie counts are deemed excessive. When I purchased a copy of Evie’s print magazine in May, I was alarmed at how the magazine not only promoted radical skinniness but also discouraged women from healthy habits like exercise. The issue explicitly told women to avoid exercise that builds muscle in “quads, hamstrings, and thighs,” on the grounds that it allegedly alienates men. The editors also discouraged women from cardio exercise, falsely claiming it will “throw your hormones off.” “A woman who is sample size looks great in virtually everything she puts on,” Evie advised, implying throughout the issue that failure to maintain a size zero could ruin your marriage, or even drive your husband to cheat. This hostility to women exercising has been accompanied by MAGA valorizing fitness as rightfully a masculine endeavor. Even members of Donald Trump’s administration, such as Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, regularly post workout videos that frame exercise as men’s work, all about grunting and showing off muscles. While it’s rare they explicitly exclude women, the lack of female bodies becomes notable if you watch enough of the videos. There is one form of exercise Evie and other right-wing influencers tacitly allow women: Pilates, a low-impact exercise similar to yoga. Pilates has a lot of benefits, but it’s not known for being especially sweaty or for building larger muscles. As The 19th reported in March, this has led to right-wing influencers extolling the “Pilates girl” as the ideal, since both strength and sweat are deemed too unfeminine. As a bonus, some on the right even claim there are no men in Pilates classes, a false claim that serves to protect fragile male egos from the possibility that a wife or girlfriend might speak to another man without supervision. But as any woman could tell you, Pilates isn’t exactly a calorie-burner. A woman who limits her exercise to Pilates will still have to subsist on very little food to get the delicate, bone-thin look these men conjure with the “Pilates girl” image. Ariana Grande is an outspoken progressive who incorporates feminist themes in her music, and she would no doubt be horrified by the way the right is using the idea of thinness to bully women into submission and self-loathing. Indeed, Grande seems distressed by the discourse around her body, and she has said she wants people to leave her alone.But this is where Jamil, perhaps in an impolitic way, is making a point that is both true and uncomfortable. Romanticizing extreme thinness contributes to eating disorders, which can do serious damage to the health of sufferers. In many cases, it might even kill them. That’s been true for decades, but now, as the issue has taken on political salience, the situation is even more alarming.Women already have an uphill battle trying to maintain a healthy body image. It’s harder now that taking basic care of yourself is demonized as being “woke.”

item.title: Max Miller tests GOP tolerance of terrible men
item.content:encoded: For Rep. Max Miller, shaking off allegations of domestic violence and child abuse should be an easy lift. The 43-year-old Ohio Republican benefits from a base that treats violence against women as a non-issue at best. In many cases, credible accusations against a GOP politician only bolsters his popularity with the MAGA base, who view men as the real victims of uppity women who should learn to keep their mouths shut. But as he aggressively attacks his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and her father, Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, Miller’s behavior is as bizarre as it is unsettling. Even Republicans are starting to squirm. Miller faces an overwhelming number of accusations from Emily Moreno, including claims that he threw hot water at his ex-wife and held a gun to her head when they were married, and that he broke his two-year-old daughter’s collarbone. An in-depth investigation from Mother Jones revealed an apparent pattern of behavior that dates back to high school, when a fellow student said Miller threw her down a flight of stairs when she refused his sexual advances. He has also been accused of violence by a college classmate and his ex-girlfriend, former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, who filed for a temporary restraining order against him on Monday. (In 2021, after Grisham published an op-ed in the Washington Post detailing abuse by her boyfriend, whom she did not name but described as a White House staffer, Miller sued her for defamation. He later dropped his suit, and the pair signed a nondisclosure agreement.)In the past, Republicans — especially Donald Trump — have successfully weathered accusations of sexual or physical violence, regardless of how many or how well-evidenced the claims, by leaning on stereotypes that paint women as petty liars.
