item.title: Preznit Fuckwit takes war advice from the Space Nazi’s Mecha-Hitler bot. Hilarity doesn’t ensue.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Almost my entire yesterday was a nightmarish hellscape of delayed flights, canceled flights, and, on top of that, delayed-and-then-canceled flights. I didn’t get home until well after 2 am.Right now I am so frazzled and sleep-deprived that there’s no way I can crank out a full-length post — so please forgive me for taking a rare day off.I’ll be back tomorrow with This Week in Stupid. Thank you for your attention to this matter.But before I go, I need to do a couple of very quick hits — New shit has come to light, man.It seems that when Donny was plotting to steal Venezuela’s oil and kidnap its leader, one of his most-trusted advisors was a janky, six-fingered plagiarism robot — but it wasn’t just plagiarism robot, oh no sirree bob. it was Grok, the Space Nazi’s own personal plagiarism robot.In December 2025, Elon Musk returned to the Oval Office for a clandestine meeting. Trump spent hours asking Grok, Musk’s AI chatbot, questions about his presidency and legacy, according to an official present.Donny spent literal hours deep in conversation with this abomination. I’ll bet you anything that he eventually forgot he wasn’t talking to a human. Naturally, Donny’s ego took over, , and he asked Mecha-Hitler if kidnapping Maduro would make him popular.At the time, Trump was ordering missile strikes against Venezuelan boats he alleged were smuggling drugs into the U.S. He asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the U.S. captured Maduro. According to the official present, the chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall. Mecha-Hitler told Donny that invading Venezuela was a totes awesome thing to do. That’s what AIs do, tell the user what they want to hear. There’s even a phrase for it: ‘AI Sycophancy.’ And it’s fucking dangerous, especially—if and when the user can no longer distinguish between genuine affirmation and performative flattery.Gee, does that sound like anyone we know? Donny’s entire White House runs on people doing performative flattery to manipulate him into doing what the want.‘Sycophantic AI’ is a thing that software engineers have had to work hard to program out of their AIs, because that shit was causing people to harm themselves — Litigation against ChatGPT claims that the chatbot systematically validated and amplified the delusions of Stein-Erik Soelberg, contributing to his committing homicide.It’s just super fucking insane that a demented imbecile in command of a nuclear arsenal is taking war advice from a six-fingered flattery-bot. Leaving Donny alone with an AI is like leaving him alone with Chucky.What could possibly go wrong?OK, here’s the other thing I want to highlight — and then, I promise I’m outta here.He’s gonna fix it. Believe in him ... all the abortion, it’s evil ... I want to see 2 people — Trump and Jesus ... we do not want Muslims taking over...I have horrible thoughts. I don't think they should be here. This isn’t their country ... they need to pack up ande go back where they came from.”I don’t even know what to say about this, except that it’s a cult — a cult made up of hateful, ignorant morons. It’s 31 days until the midterms. We need to out-vote these shitheads, and take away their power.Well, it’s Friday — and we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.here are two from the 1980s, taken by Ms Spouse’s bestie Mandi.Have a great Friday, everyone. My god, I really suck at taking the day off. Look, this one’s only 867 words. that’s like half a day off, so there’s that.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Free ebook from Chicago: Plundered Skulls and Stolen Spirits
item.author: 554127793.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
item.content:encoded:
Who owns the past and the objects that physically connect us to history? And who has the right to decide this ownership, particularly when the objects are sacred or, in the case of skeletal remains, human? Is it the museums that care for the objects or the communities whose ancestors made them? These questions are at the heart of , an unflinching insider account by a leading curator who has spent years learning how to balance these controversial considerations.
Five decades ago, Native American leaders launched a crusade to force museums to return their sacred objects and allow them to rebury their kin. Today, hundreds of tribes use the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act to help them recover their looted heritage from museums across the country. As senior curator of anthropology at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science, Chip Colwell has navigated firsthand the questions of how to weigh the religious freedom of Native Americans against the academic freedom of scientists and whether the emptying of museum shelves elevates human rights or destroys a common heritage. This book offers his personal account of the process of repatriation, following the trail of four objects as they were created, collected, and ultimately returned to their sources: a sculpture that is a living god, the scalp of a massacre victim, a ceremonial blanket, and a skeleton from a tribe considered by some to be extinct. These specific stories reveal a dramatic process that involves not merely obeying the law, but negotiating the blurry lines between identity and morality, spirituality and politics.
Things, like people, have biographies. Repatriation, Colwell argues, is a difficult but vitally important way for museums and tribes to acknowledge that fact—and heal the wounds of the past while creating a respectful approach to caring for these rich artifacts of history.

item.title: It’s Time To Separate The Real Teams From The Clowns
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: We're in the middle of bye season now, which means some of your favorites—Texas, UCLA, Duke, Utah and others—are receiving well-deserved weeks off that will allow their fan bases to forget who they hate the most. Well, not forget, really, but maybe forget to mention for at least a few days. No coaches have been fired yet, but now that we're in October, the time is rapidly approaching where a lot of professional Football Men will be given an opportunity to start spending more time with their families. Apologies to those families for what will befall them.The rest of the week, though, should be about small moves among big teams, as the upward funnel begins to gain suction and the power teams begin to sort themselves out. Margin of victory will start mattering less as simple victory begins to suffice, and the number of undefeated teams will shrink from its current total of 22 (out of 138, roughly 15 percent). The most intriguing of those teams might be North Dakota State, freshly escaped from dispensing ritual thumpings in the Missouri Valley and released into the allegedly more hostile environs of the Mountain West. They may even make a case for a playoff berth, provided the sentient oil stains on the committee deign to notice them. For the moment, they have to worry about Wyoming, as do we all.

item.title: The Too-Small Lynx Will Have To Answer Some Big Questions
item.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
item.content:encoded: As end-of-season Minnesota Lynx press conferences go, this year’s was pretty subdued. There was no “shit was stolen from us,” no missives delivered against Cathy Engelbert. “I don’t have a speech prepared, so everyone can relax,” Napheesa Collier said at the start of her exit interview Thursday afternoon. After an 87-71 loss to the New York Liberty in Game 2 of the first round of the playoffs, the eliminated Lynx are just looking inward. The Liberty, set to the play the Atlanta Dream in the second round starting Sunday, became the first No. 8 seed to knock out a No. 1 seed in the first round. “It sucks,” was all Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve had to say about that distinction after the loss Tuesday night. It probably doesn’t deserve more analysis than that. The strength of this particular No. 8 seed is one reason: The Liberty are a veteran, playoff-tested team still led by one of the greatest players of all time. And in a way it did not a few years ago, when three-quarters of a 12-team league made the playoffs, it does also take a little more accomplishment to appear in the WNBA postseason these days. The last time the Liberty were a No. 8 seed, in 2021, they made the playoffs with a 12-20 record. This year, with a 26-18 record, they finished just seven games back of the Lynx, while eight games separated the Liberty and No. 9 Portland.Beyond unfortunate history, the first-round loss makes for a sooner-than-expected start to what might be the league’s most interesting offseason. The thought on everyone's mind Tuesday night and again at Minnesota's media availability Thursday was something like: Two's a coincidence, three's a trend. Why has the Lynx season ended in heartbreak for three straight years?

item.title: Jack Smith Did Not Conspire Against Donald Trump While Watching Steph Curry Score 60 Points In An Overtime Loss To The Hawks
item.author: David Roth
item.content:encoded: The most salient part of the accusation that Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt lodged against former special prosecutor Jack Smith in a Senate hearing on Tuesday is that it was wrong. It was ecstatically and grandiosely wrong, and obviously wrong in ways that even a rudimentary blog-level fact check would have caught. It was wrong in ways that would only be possible at this particular low ebb in American political and broader executive function—based on unverified and unvetted information given only to Republican senators by the Department of Justice, too hastily put to oafish misuse by well-credentialed chumps of roughly equal laziness and ambition in the pursuit of a spiteful but otherwise opaque end.In that sense, it is extremely familiar. If it hadn't ended with Schmitt dangling upside down and blustering like the previously undiscovered suburban version of Yosemite Sam after becoming ensnared in his own malfunctioning perjury trap, it might not even have been news at all. In absolute terms, it was as stupid as more or less anything that's happened on the floor of the United States Senate in a century or so, a half-assed 16x-speed gloss on McCarthyism from people who do not really know what that or anything else was, and whose attention spans have left them incapable of parsing even your wordier memes. In relative terms, this is just what our government is like much of the time.It is not difficult to see what Schmitt was trying to do, and it is extremely easy to see how and why he and his staff of pale and chittering Renfields screwed it up. That failure is grounded in a tragicomic lack of Ball Knowledge, but also in either a more overtly comic inattention to detail, an aversion to even light investigative work, or both. Schmitt et al went through the DOJ's dump of Smith's text messages and believed they had found evidence of him secretly attending an Atlanta Hawks home game against the Golden State Warriors on Feb. 3, 2024. Accusing someone of attending a Hawks game is rude on the merits, but neither libelous nor scandalous in its own right; why Schmitt believed this was newsworthy, let alone a suitably bouncy springboard to soft-launch his own vice presidential ambitions, is something else entirely.

item.title: Yet More …
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: We’re seeing article after article now restating in slightly different ways the same basic point about the AI infrastructure boom: how will this level of investment ever be recouped? This new article in the Journal is entitled: Will America Spend 9% of Its GDP on AI? The Industry Is Counting on It. (It references the same Brookings study we discussed a week ago.) This is more or less the same story as I flagged in that Bain report in last night’s post. A market of $6 trillion for AI by 2031; 9% of GDP in 2032. The numbers may be based on slightly different global modelings — just how much investment, rates of return, etc. But they’re mostly different ways of stating the staggering growth that will be required to cover current levels of capital expenditure. The Journal notes that 9% of GDP in 2032 (one year later than the Bain & Co report focuses on) will mean Americans are spending as much on AI as food, half as much as they will spend on health care. The Journal article reminds us that this isn’t simply about adoption and new products. You have to factor in what will likely be rapidly falling prices as well as competition from new entrants with possibly far lower sunk costs and debt.Getting into the particulars involves so many variables it’s hard make sense of it without an economic degree. But the overall story is the same as the one in the Bain study. Silicon Valley has committed the economy to unimaginable levels of investment in a very promising but still largely unproven technology. And now we have to go on a national crash course of maniacal innovation just to get out from under that spending overhang or the whole economy craters. Of course, if AI just does a million amazing things and makes all our lives happier and more fun … well, we’ll have to really thank them. But this seems uncertain.

item.title: The Wuppertal Schwebebahn Is Real And It Is My Friend
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: When my friend in Cologne asked me if I might want to take a day trip, thanks to Cologne's proximity to various other notable cities (Dortmund, Düsseldorf, Bonn, among others), I said that I would like to go to Wuppertal to ride the Schwebebahn. To which they said, "I that's what you were going to say." My brand is strong.Before my trip to Germany, I declared this desire to ride the Wuppertal Schwebebahn to many of my close friends, and also several strangers. Some people thought it sounded pretty cool. Others said they were happy for me. More than once I was accused of making up words.Nothing about the glorious feat that is the Wuppertal Schwebebahn is made up. "Schwebebahn" means suspended railway, or literally "floating train," which is an apt way to describe a dangling monorail. It was the design of German engineer Eugen Langen and opened along and above the river Wupper in 1901, connecting several towns that would eventually merge to form the city of Wuppertal, or literally "Wupper valley." Both the early look of the train and its surroundings are captured in footage shot from the front of the Schwebebahn in 1902. Behold, "The Flying Train."

item.title: Igor Shesterkin Caught His White Whale And Scored A Goalie Goal
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: The thing about all goalie goals is that they rock. There are roughly 175 feet and six prideful skaters between the promised land and any netminder bold enough to even attempt to reach it. There have been but 21 goalie goals, scored by 18 different goalies, in the entire history of the NHL. The thing about Thursday night's goalie goal, specifically, is that no goalie since Ron Hextall has ever so clearly wanted it more than Igor Shesterkin.He is also exceedingly deserving. He is in that classic New York Ranger situation of being one of the league's elite stoppers, trapped on a team that does not seem capable of building a commensurate roster around him. Surely he thinks about how Henrik Lundqvist retired without a Cup. Surely he should get a little treat from time to time, something just for Igor. Often—notably often—that treat-seeking looks like firing a puck down the ice at an empty net. He does it so often that home crowds start anticipating the attempt as soon as the opposing goalie heads to the bench. He does it so often that Kenny Albert predicted it 10 minutes before it happened last night. And he has comesoclose. “I feel like probably a dozen times I’ve been on the bench thinking, ‘OK, this one goes in,’ and he barely misses,” said Mika Zibanejad. Shesterkin has said he scored one in juniors and has been chasing that high ever since. But he never found paydirt until last night.

item.title: Mr. Monk And The Unfinished Book
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: One of Monk's most Monk-like episodes in all of occurs in Season 2, Episode 7: "Mr. Monk and the Sleeping Suspect." Adrian Monk, Tony Shalhoub's impersonation of Eeyore if the donkey had severe OCD, has taken to visiting Brian Babbage, a comatose man and his prime murder suspect, for an unofficial therapy session. Monk's actual therapist is away on vacation, and the private detective desperately needs someone to talk to. "He's a good listener," Monk tells his bewildered assistant, Sharona Fleming.Monk sits by Babbage's hospital bed and spills his many woes while doing what he does best: puttering around and noticing things. Monk notices Babbage's watch is a couple minutes fast—an unacceptable misalignment in his world—and as he fixes the watch, he notices a bit of glue stuck to the face. "What were you gluing?" Monk wonders aloud. Suddenly, a distant clatter causes Monk to whirl around and knock over a flowerpot, spilling dirt on the floor. Such disorder, the viewer knows, is unacceptable to Monk, who promptly fetches a vacuum to clean it up. Trusty wet wipe in hand, Monk unplugs a white cord from an outlet to plug in the vacuum and starts sucking up the dirt. The noise of the vacuum is almost loud enough to obscure the fact that Monk has just unplugged Babbage from life support. The man flatlines, but Monk plugs him back in and manages to restart his heart with CPR. Monk has, per his , both wrecked and saved the day. The scene then cuts to a disgruntled outsider, a nurse, who, like many, disapproves of the Monkness of it all.Monk's improbable theory—that a man who was literally comatose while the murder happened was, in fact, the murderer—turns out to be right, of course. Brian Babbage had mailed bombs to his siblings so that he alone would inherit their late father's riches. The glue was the clue: The smear on Babbage's watch was evidence of how he glued the bombs inside blue mailboxes so that the packages would drop down and ship months later, after the adhesive degraded. And it turns out that Babbage's near-death experience—his second one, really—actually restarted his heart, allowing the police to confirm his guilt and arrest him.

item.title: Who’s That Guy? 2026 MLB postseason edition
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: There’s no one on the Dodgers at this point who deserves "Who’s That Guy?" treatment. If they have a new face in the mix at all, it will be highly touted prospect Josue De Paula, off the bench. And yet they have the ultimate example of a player who makes viewers utter the question.Kiké Hernández is pretty solidly this generation’s most disproportionate October scene-stealer — he’s That Guy in the same way as an actor with no starring credits but a hundred memorable bit character roles. He’s a player whose baseball fan Q score is entirely dependent on your postseason consumption.All those roles have earned him serious screen time. Hernández has taken more postseason plate appearances (328) than all but eight players since his debut 11 years ago. In that playing time? He has been Good. His .826 OPS is 15th among the 49 hitters who have taken at least 150 trips to the plate in the same span — behind 13 guys for whom the Hall of Fame is or was at one point a reasonable possibility, and Randy Arozarena. He’s three points ahead of Aaron Judge.Who’s that guy? He’s someone who has made the most of the biggest moments. Over and over. Everyone else on this list would be thrilled to join him, even just once.The bulk of today’s newsletter is devoted to players who might make their names nationally known over the next month or so, who might go from unheralded to hero, from promising to the prince who was promised. Will I ever match the inaugural edition of this exercise from 2020, in which I picked out mostly anonymous, hotel-quarantined, push-up-performing, cowboy-boot-wearing Arozarena as a potential playoff difference-maker? Almost certainly not! But we press on anyway.Thanks to The War On Drugs for creating a soundtrack specifically for this segment.Victor Mesa Jr., Rays outfielderEven after a pretty unimpeachable 98-win season to stun the competition in a rugged AL East, it’s understandable if the Rays lineup doesn’t jump out at you. Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz, Jonathan Aranda, trade deadline addition Liam Hicks, and then who?Victor Mesa Jr., that’s who.If you’d heard of Mesa prior to this year, it was probably as the second fiddle to his ballyhooed brother Victor Victor Mesa. The Marlins signed both of them out of Cuba back in 2018, but this Victor Mesa (singular, second of his name) surpassed his sibling and gradually worked his way up through the minors. The Rays got him in a trade in February, brought him up for his MLB debut in May and benefited as he established himself as a key piece of their lineup, batting .260 with 14 homers and nine steals in 79 games.The postseason amps up the competition level. The precise contours of that shift are difficult to put under the microscope, but one is very apparent: A greater share of all pitches will be zipping in faster. Being able to handle premium velocity is not everything, but it’s a nice trait when push comes to shove in October, one shared by some of the era’s most durable postseason bats: Bryce Harper, Max Muncy, Yordan Alvarez, etc.So I took note that, among all hitters who saw at least 75 pitches over 97 mph in 2026, Mesa registered the best results, slashing .412/.524/.941 with three long balls. He’s also coming in red hot, with a 184 wRC+ in September ranking as a top 15 mark in the majors.Garrett Mitchell, Brewers outfielderLet me put this as plainly as possible: Mitchell is an absolute athletic freak. If Statcast were sentient, it would be making googly eyes at him from across the bar.The problem has been actualizing those physical gifts on the field. Mitchell might just be Byron Buxton Lite. At age 28, he finally played a full-ish season. It went pretty well! He homered 11 times, stole 14 bags and played good if unspectacular defense in center field. His hyperdrive swing is pretty locked into a path, perhaps hindering his ability to make contact and contributing to a high strikeout rate, but he also upped his walk rate and reached base at a .354 clip. Pretty useful!Healthy and leading off for another dynamite Brewers team, there’s a good chance Mitchell throws up sparks.Adrián Morejón, Padres pitcherMason Miller is the headliner in San Diego’s monster bullpen, but the left-handed Morejón is more than a supporting act. Over the past three years, Morejón has thrown more innings in relief than anyone in baseball, while also being one of the 10 most dominant arms working out of the bullpen, by Fielding Independent Pitching’s accounting of strikeouts, walks and homers.If the Padres run into crucial moments before the eighth inning, expect Morejón (or Bradgley Rodriguez) to get the nod.George Lombard Jr., Yankees shortstopSince no one has ever gotten out over their skis about a young Yankees shortstop, I think it’s safe to dream on Lombard Jr. as he is thrust into the spotlight in pinstripes.The 21-year-old major-league scion forced his way to the Bronx with power potential, a mature approach — on-base percentage across three minor-league levels: .411 — and defensive savvy. He understandably hasn’t mastered that approach at the big-league level just yet, but you can see flashes of his aptitude. Four hits and three runs against the Red Sox was a roaring start.If he mans a solid shortstop and keeps his strikeouts in check, he’s going to have plaudits and expectations following him like paparazzi.Tyler Mahle, Braves pitcherPerhaps the under-the-radar deadline move of the year, Mahle posted a 1.99 ERA for the Braves after running up a 5.13 mark for the Giants. Neither the great nor the bad was totally reflective of his efforts, but the 32-year-old has altered his formula a little since the deal, boosting his splitter usage to career highs.His continued good form is wildly important for Atlanta’s hopes of advancing any further. It’s essentially Chris Sale, Mahle and then a blurred line between swingmen, openers and bulk guys. Even in an eventual loss, his seven strong innings in Wild Card Game 2 kept the Braves’ pitching corps strong enough to win Game 3.If Mahle is asked to make the same bold stand against the Dodgers, he’ll have a chance to redefine his workmanlike career into something else entirely.Hagen Smith, White Sox pitcherWith a time machine and a healthy appreciation for trickery, you could really mess with White Sox fans by going back to 2024 and telling them that their newest top five draft pick would start a postseason Game 1 within three years.That statement is technically true now, as Smith opened their Wild Card Series romp over the Astros, but not yet spiritually accurate. The lefty has reached the majors as a reliever, with iffy command still hampering excellent stuff. Yet as he found his footing in the bullpen, he improved, throwing down MLB’s fifth-best strikeout rate in September.He’s a boom or bust proposition, but nonetheless looks like one of the best options available to manager Will Venable. It’s first-round talent, something you don’t need a time machine to see.Angel Martinez, Guardians outfielderThe Guardians, believe it or not, had the best second-half offense of any team remaining in the American League side of the bracket, per park-adjusted wRC+. Steven Kwan and Chase DeLauter were the biggest reasons for their run-scoring prowess, but the lineup is longer on threats than it might appear. Maybe.Martinez was great down the stretch, batting .310/.346/.559 after Aug. 1, good for a 152 wRC+ that was “between Bryce Harper and Yordan Alvarez” good.Did the underlying numbers support such production? No, no they did not. Martinez will swing at almost anything, but he does usually make contact, and he does usually scoop that contact into the air to the pull side. He is nothing if not a man of action, and sometimes that’s enough. ⚾️An arbitrary Bandwagon fan ranking of the remaining teamsEvery remaining team ranked by their attractiveness as a narrative foil for the Dodgers:Padres: Little brother bets his life savings he can jump his bike over the house into the pool, then somehow does itBrewers: What if Moneyball had a happy ending?White Sox: Downtrodden soul is suddenly emboldened by GodYankees: Old money reasserts dominanceRays: What if Moneyball had a sequel that had a happy ending?Guardians: Tortoise beats hare, but if speed were home runs or somethingBraves: Rival takes out more accomplished rivalDodgers: A true champion’s only competition comes from withinThe 2026 Red Sox were bad, and then amazing, and then they were just … fine. And fine doesn’t tend to cut it in the playoffs. It did not cut it at Yankee Stadium this week, and the good feelings of their amazing win streak dissolved into rancor.Chad Tracy, no longer just the interim manager, is in the loud, squishy muck of disappointment after the Red Sox let both games get away from them shortly after pulling their starting pitchers. Neither Payton Tolle in Game 1 nor Sonny Gray in Game 2 were winning their duels with Yankees aces Cam Schlittler and Max Fried, but their departures registered as early and preceded big Yankees hits.After it all, the veteran Gray expressed his problem directly.“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time,” Gray told reporters. “I think that’s a fact. I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am. I think you can probably ask the (players), and they felt the same way.”I don’t think either decision had a clear cut answer, though I admittedly preferred Gray over Erik Miller for a second straight day in Game 2. But any hope for a rational discussion of those nebulous, uncertain calculations was dashed when Willson Contreras said the magic words to summon Tired Baseball Discourse, complaining that players “have computers telling you what to do.”This should blow over. It would be more concerning if a clubhouse full of players frustrated and a little angry minutes after their season ended. But this being Boston, and the tone of these comments being pointed, it also seems two days in the Bronx could scrub the Red Sox all the way back to April, to the offseason, to the raised eyebrows and skeptical glances directed at top baseball executive Craig Breslow and his front office.It will all be different come spring, yet it might not feel much different until there’s a more powerful memory to override these repeated shortcomings. This resilient summer felt like it might be just that, until it didn’t.The Padres chewed up the Cubs and spat them out, much to the delight of a raucous crowd at Petco Park. Fernando Tatis Jr. blasted a homer on the first pitch of the bottom of the first inning in Game 1, the ball slipping just over the glove of a soaring Pete Crow-Armstrong, and it really just devolved from there.Padres starter Michael King sliced and diced them in Game 1, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh. Then, as the fans chanted the Don Orsillo home run call “Holy Sheets” in Game 2 …Gavin Sheets complied. And the Cubs never got off the mat.Despite the emergence of Crow-Armstrong as the obvious NL MVP, a true superstar, the Cubs are teetering over an abyss of an offseason with a bevy of impending free agents and a dearth of apparent answers to the resulting holes.Re-signing and/or replacing all of the talent sloughing off this roster will be hugely expensive. The Cubs don't have great alternatives, though, given the state of their farm system. Their margin for error next year is thinner than it would have been if they'd been less aggressive at the deadline, too, as Brett Bateman (outfield), Moisés Ballesteros (DH) and Jefferson Rojas(infield) all could have been reinforcements for the roster if they hadn't been dealt away. The front office recognized the importance of capitalizing on the year they were getting from Crow-Armstrong and on the last prime-adjacent years of Bregman, Swanson, Happ, Suzuki and more. They pushed in their chips. After Wednesday night, it sure feels like they lost the hand, but playing it was the brave (and perhaps the only) thing to do.It’s still too early to draw conclusions about the postseason’s effect on challenge strategy — or challenge emotions — but the tension is clearly high.“What we’ve made clear,” Venable, the White Sox manager, told The Athletic, “the worst thing that can happen is that we get to the end of the game, we have two challenges left and we’ve missed a bunch of opportunities to use our challenges.”

item.title: Why top Texas election denier Ken Paxton could cause chaos if he loses his Senate race
item.author: 1axb4tfa76e59b2esfskm9005uz0lpny82asbn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: It’s October, Halloween is coming, and I can’t think of anything more frightening than the enormous federal resources that Trump has directed to try to prove that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him. (OK, maybe “The Blair Witch Project” or “The Exorcist” are scarier — but at least those are only movies).Luckily, the horror show that is the Trump administration’s effort to find mass voter fraud and relitigate the 2020 election has fallen flat. With all the chaos and noise Trump and his allies are creating around the midterms, it’s easy to forget that the election deniers are losing.But this week was a good reminder: Not one, but two Trump administration officials tasked at least in part with proving 2020 voter conspiracies abruptly resigned — and both quit without proving anything. First was Kurt Olsen, a hardcore Trump loyalist who led a special White House task force probing 2020 election conspiracies, then moved to the Department of Justice.The other was Andrew Bailey, a former Missouri attorney general and avowed election denier, who was the FBI's co-deputy director and helped lead the bureau’s raid on a Fulton County, Georgia election hub earlier this year.They’re the latest in a string of resignations of administration appointees who were brought in to prove 2020 election conspiracy theories, or indict the president’s political enemies, and utterly failed to do so. Nearly half a dozen election deniers recently resigned — and there’s still no evidence that the 2020 election was rigged.

item.title: Shinichi Atobe
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Shinichi Atobe, a Japanese electronic musician from Saitama. We’ve recommended his music afewtimesbefore. He’s been making quality techno/house music, beasting in the underground since the start of the millennium. In a conversation with Tone Glow, he said, “I started making techno when I was 27. At the time, I was working as a security guard. I saved up money to buy a Prophet 600. I was listening to a variety of techno music.” We’re playing his latest album, , which came out in March. It carries on his style of laid back techno, with drums keeping the pace and synths conveying his signature form of energized calm. We’re also playing from 2018, which to our ears is his magnum opus.Have a fantastic weekend.

item.title: Raymond Zeitler: What is spook?
item.author: Raymond Zeitler
item.content:encoded:
The Emacs function is not what you think it is. It doesn't make creepy noises, draw scary ASCII art or change the theme to orange on black. In fact it has nothing at all to do with Halloween, ghosts, monsters, pandemics or IRS audits.
What it does is insert words and phrases into the current buffer "to help give your message ... attractiveness for automated keyword scanners."
What kind of words or phrases might you expect to see? To find out I invoked while composing this content. Here's what it added:
TELINT Drug North Korea Security Consulting Virii Abu Ghraib Fort Hancock CUD AMEMB Vaccine MARTA racal E.O.D. Blizzard Nigeria
It's easy to configure spook to insert an alternate set of words and phrases -- just change the file name in the variable from "spook.lines" to the name of the alternate file. Unfortunately it must reside in the Emacs data directory; the file's location is fixed. The variable can be found in the Spook customization group, whose parent group is Games.
Even with only 72 lines in its source code file, spook demonstrates how to insert one or more random lines from a file into the current buffer. It's "easy" if you have Administrator permissions. The 72 lines is the entire spook.el file; the first 48% of the file provides the usual comments that describe the GNU GPL, author, maintainer info as well as documentation.

item.title: Bain Company Brainstorms Where The AI Revenue’s Gonna Come From
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: A friend sent me this new Bain & Company study on the growth required to match the current levels of capital expenditure on AI, essentially breaking down the cost of the data center and other associated build outs. It’s an interesting document, not simply for the number-crunching and the predictions, but as a document in the more literary and analytic sense. Needless to say, Bain isn’t coming at this from any “boo capitalism!”/”this is insane lol” viewpoint. But the conclusions aren’t that far from the “this is insane lol” position. It’s very much, “hey! we can do this” but also, “um … wow, there’s quite a lot to do.”The broad stroke numbers are these. The study says that to keep up with the current levels of capital expenditures AI will need to become a $6 trillion dollar market by 2031. (To give some perspective on that number, a recent Gartner study predicted that global IT spending will be just under $6.4 trillion this year. So devices, hardware, software, services, kind of everything.) It then posits that we can see the beginnings of, with some level of out-year predictability, something on the order of a $1.5 trillion market — which would be made up of a greatly expanded consumer market (Claude apps, ChatGPT, etc.) of between $200 and $400 billion and then an enterprise market (software, sales, marketing, business optimization) of between $1 and $1.4 trillion. So we’re left with about $4.5 trillion to go. That’s where the crash course in innovation comes in.

item.title: The Roberts Court Re-Opens But It’s Been Open for Business and Trump All Along
item.author: Lisa Graves
item.content:encoded: The first Monday in October marks the official opening of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2026 term, but in many ways, the Roberts Court never really left.Sure, Chief Justice John Roberts took some time by the shore of the private island off the coast of Maine where he owns not one but two summer homes, and the other justices took their own posh vacations, too. But Roberts and his fellow Republican appointees were also busy responding to Donald Trump’s repeated cries of “emergency” whenever impartial lower court judges temporarily blocked his destructive desires.I suppose we shouldn’t be shocked that, like millions of Americans, Roberts worked from home. Unlike most people, however, his home was his second and third residences, side by side on the water in Penobscot Bay. After all, Roberts is the richest justice on the nation’s highest court, with a fortune that has grown in part through his wife’s work placing elite lawyers at prestigious law firms, many of which have business before the Court. In August, a couple dozen peaceful protesters—and one sea-faring dog—kayaked in front of Roberts’s waterfront places to hold a “By Land and By Sea” vigil. They carried signs saying “Roberts Benched the Constitution” and “The Roberts Court: A Rubber-Stamp for Fascism.”Those signs were printed before the Court’s latest decree, which overturned a lower court order temporarily blocking the Trump administration’s efforts to deport people to third countries they have never been to, without giving them a meaningful opportunity to contest being sent somewhere they might be tortured or killed. That policy sure sounds like something a fascist would do, and the Roberts Court’s action sure looks like a rubber stamp.Lawyers for the immigrants being targeted by Trump told the Court that the administration’s claims of harm—which amount to whining about the inconvenience of waiting and the alleged expense of canceled flights—“ignore the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime U.S. residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there.”The cowards in the Republican majority of the Roberts Court refused to attach individual names to the opinion that at least one of them or their clerks actually wrote. Instead, the Court issued the decree “per curiam,” which traditionally means unanimous, even though three justices—Sotomayor, Jackson, and Kagan—dissented.Again, the Republican-appointed justices intervened to protect a Republican MAGA policy, allowing a potentially deadly plan to proceed while the Court waits to hear oral arguments in December. A final ruling could come as far as nine months from now.Meanwhile, thanks to the Court’s aggressive intervention in his favor, Trump can continue sending an untold number of people to 29 other countries, including:South Sudan, where the U.S. State Department has issued a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” warning due to the deadly Ebola outbreak, stating that “Americans should not travel [there] for any reason,”Rwanda, which has a Level 3 “Reconsider Travel” warning (and Level 4 for parts of the country due to a regional genocidal civil war), andEswatini, which has a Level 2 caution from the State Department and is an absolute monarchy where the king has imprisoned journalists and pro-democracy activists.The ruling that John Roberts, Sam Alito, Clarence Thomas, Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett signed off on without signing shocks the conscience.As the award-winning outlet reported, the Roberts Court has now passed a milestone no other Supreme Court has: “For the first time, it decided more cases by secret ballot, and with few signed opinions, than it did for cases argued in open court.” In other words, it has been using the shadowy shadow docket to remake our laws and implicitly overturn legal precedents that lower court judges have faithfully followed, displacing the detailed factual findings of trial court judges. Almost all of this has been in aid of Trump, the man John Roberts concocted criminal immunity for after Trump unleashed the worst attack on the U.S. Capitol since the War of 1812 in an effort to subvert the 2020 election.The dozens of rulings for Trump since Roberts administered the presidential oath of office in 2025—when Trump claimed he would protect and defend the Constitution—have further aggrandized his power. He has since run rampant, decimating federal agencies, diverting congressional budget allocations for public health, laying siege to American cities, selling out our resources, and dictating so much more.Yet now we are supposed to believe that the Roberts Court took up the climate case because it has fair-minded intentions? As with the Trump cases, the Court did not have to accept the appeal by Suncor and Exxon challenging the suit against them in Colorado state court.The Roberts Court chose to take up that case because at least four justices wanted to—and presumably thought they had five votes—to help the oil companies escape potential liability under state law. I am glad that Sam Alito recused himself from the case. In my view, the federal recusal statute required him to do so because he is personally invested in an array of fossil fuel stocks that would benefit from a ruling for Suncor and Exxon.But I worry that his belated recusal means that the other justices in his faction don’t need his vote to prevail and so him remaining on the case would muddy the waters and taint the coverage of the eventual ruling.In research I spearheaded this summer, we documented that Alito previously made up to nearly $250,000 from his Exxon holdings alone (enough to help buy his waterfront summer home in New Jersey). We also found that his fossil fuel holdings have increased his wealth by as much as $2.9 million since his appointment to the Court.Come Monday, we are supposed to believe that the oral argument—where Trump’s gravelly mouthpiece, John Sauer, will argue on the side of the oil companies—is not a kind of theatre and that the justices’ minds are not already made up. Alito’s belated recusal did nothing to prevent him from discussing the case with the other justices for the past year. Before now, he could discuss any or all of the briefs, including numerous amicus briefs from groups funded by fossil fuel billionaire Charles Koch and billionaire trustee Leonard Leo. Leo has long cultivated Big Oil donors to the Federalist Society: Koch and his company, Gold Circle donor Chevron, and dozens of lawyers and law firms that represent the oil majors and related industries.And after all of this—including the reality that no federal law preempts states from hearing climate tort cases against corporations—we are supposed to accept that five judges on the Supreme Court, who are totally unaccountable to us, get to dictate our ability to hold oil companies accountable. Exxon literally knew that burning fossil fuels was altering our atmosphere and harming the viability of life on our planet.I, for one, refuse to accept that fate.That’s the fate John Roberts presumes he can dictate. Shortly after he was confirmed, he told C-Span that if the American people don’t like what his court does, “it’s just too bad.”It’s more than too bad. It’s a disaster for our country and our world. And I am determined to do everything within the law and within my power to rebuke and reform the Roberts Court, and repair the grave damage it has done to our democracy and our future.We can chart a new path and we must. The first step is to be clear-eyed about what the Roberts Court is and what it is not. It is not a fair court. It is acting as an arm—and indeed an armament—of the powerful, against the public interest of the American people, almost every time it rules.What I’m Reading or Rereading:I am reading through all of the and look forward to letting you know what I uncover about the financial ties of the array of front and dark money groups echoing Big Oil’s claims.Since I have been recovering from emergency surgery, I have also been reading every day for enjoyment and for a little daily guidance and encouragement. My latest find is .And, —specifically the exceptions clause, which allows Congress to set the types of cases the Supreme Court can hear beyond the ones it must hear, such as disputes between states over their borders.What’s really happening at the Supreme Court?Join COURIER and Americans United on for Weaponizing Faith: Christian Nationalism at the Supreme Court. Featuring Rachel Laser, Stasha M. Rhodes, Michael Podhorzer, and moderator Lisa Graves, this panel uncovers how political allies are reshaping our legal system and what we must do to reclaim it.Attend in person at The Milton Theatre in D.C. or watch the live stream online. RSVP today!Get the full receipts every Monday in The Cover-UpAccountability starts with the record. COURIER’s new Contradictions Tracker compares testimony to the Epstein files, with every source linked. Follow along every Monday in The Cover-Up.

I was trying to see why teams are blitzing more this year, even setting aside blitz maven Brian Flores (his Vikings defense is currently blitzing at a mind-boggling 76.9 percent for the season, according to PFF) and former Flores assistant Daronte Jones, now defensive coordinator at Washington (the Commanders are second in blitz rate at 52.1 percent).In 2026, it turns out that teams that already loved to blitz are the ones blitzing more—median and bottom-fifth percentile blitz rates have not increased by any amount over the last few seasons. item.title: Trump DOJ Doubles Down on Attacking Judges
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Blanche Targets Minnesota JudgesUnder the pretext of an ethics complaint against all but one of the active federal judges in Minnesota, Attorney General Todd Blanche signaled yesterday that not only will the Trump administration continue to run roughshod over the judicial branch but that judges had better shut up about it.The complaint filed by second and third highest ranking DOJ officials with the uber-right-wing 8th Circuit Court of Appeals is ostensibly about an admittedly unusual decision by the federal judges who bore the brunt of Operation Metro Surge to sit for an interview with the New York Times for a story that ran Sept. 17.In the interview, the judges — including Patrick Schiltz who was the chief judge during the peak of the flood of mass deportation cases swamping the Minnesota federal court — defended the rule of law, provided a civics lesson on the role of the courts, and described the structural and institutional challenges they had faced. They refrained from talking about individual cases, but they did speak in broad terms about the habeas cases in general, Operation Metro Surge and the conduct of the Trump DOJ.The complaint — signed by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter and Associate Attorney General Stan Woodward — accused the judges of pandering to the press and engaging in unethical behavior that “flagrantly violated” the canons of judicial ethics. It specifically called out Judge Schiltz and Judge John R. Tunheim — who were both quoted by name in the NYT article — for what it called “particularly egregious” misconduct.The Trump DOJ asked the 8th Circuit to appoint a special committee to conduct an investigation of the judges for their allegedly improper behavior and to order Judges Schiltz and Tunheim to recuse themselves from any cases involving DHS.The Trump DOJ getting on its high horse about legal ethics is a lot to take on its own. But it’s also striking that the complaint leans into what DOJ officials see as a friendly audience on the 8th Circuit. It emphasizes, for instance, the appeals court’s own decision upholding the Trump administration’s mass detention policy without bond — one of only two appeals courts to do so — in which it overruled the Minnesota judges.Traditionally, Article III judges have been free to speak publicly on matters of judicial administration, the Constitution, democracy — civics, if you will. They have been free to lobby for more funding, better security protection, restructuring of the judiciary, and reform measures without running afoul of ethics requirements.But the Trump DOJ — which has defied orders left and right, hidden its worst conduct behind unprepared junior lawyers, botched cases, fired huge numbers of experienced attorneys, and made a hash of the distinguished department — now wants to clamp down on the ability of judges to stand up against what may be the most sustained assault on the judiciary in the nation’s history.SCOTUS Takes Up Mass DetentionsAs expected, the Supreme Court will take up the Trump administration’s policy of mass detention without bond that the circuit courts have split on, but which dozens of judges in thousands of cases have found to be unlawful.The family of Renee Good who was shot and killed by ICE in January during Operation Metro Surge has filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration arising from her death.Broadview Six Hearing This AfternoonA federal judge in Chicago this afternoon will hear arguments over whether to conduct a further inqury into alleged misconduct into Trump’s DOJ’s handling of the grand jury in the Broadview Six case and the aftermath of that now-abandoned prosecution of ICE protesters.The Supreme Court’s prior handling of the third-country removal case was already the most troublesome emergency docket case, Georgetown law professor Steve Vladeck argues, then came this week’s unexplained decision in the case:“There have certainly been rulings on the emergency docket that I believe to be more clearly and obviously wrong on the merits. And there have been rulings on the emergency docket that have produced even more harmful effects domestically and/or to the separation of powers. But there’s something profoundly ugly about the D.V.D. case that, unfortunately, was on display again on Tuesday.”Cannon Wiggles Out of BindGive her credit: Judge Aileen Cannon has gotten out of the pickle she was in on Volume II of former Special Counsel Jack Smith’s report. She struck a motion from FBI agents who investigated the Mar-a-Lago documents case and are now being targeted by the Trump DOJ seeking clarification on her order sealing Volume II. Her reason: The lawyers had failed to confer with the co-defendants in the underlying criminal case about their motion before filing it.11th Circuit Stirs to ActionIn the Volume II case which is on appeal, the 11th Circuit the appeals court rescheduled oral arguments yet again but moved them earlier for the first time after months of kicking the can down the road. Instead of January of next year they’re now scheduled for the first week of November. Nothing much going on that week.Reflecting Pool Case Dismissed With PrejudiceRuling that “no crime occurred,” a DC judge has ruled that the already-dismissed Reflecting Pool case against David Hearn should be dismissed with prejudice, meaning the Trump DOJ can’t bring the case against him again in the future.“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era. There is no precedent.”—Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, on last night’s horrific attempted execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee.Pike remains hospitalized this morning. Gov. Bill Lee (R) has halted executions through the end of the year.

item.title: Nation Of Bondholders
item.author: Michael Waters
item.content:encoded: It turns out you can trace America’s 2008 financial crash, in a roundabout way, to 18th-century Prussia. The Seven Years’ War left the kingdom in financial shambles: Just to afford the fighting, Prussia’s king, Frederick the Great, had hired private minters to ramp up currency production. So in 1769, Frederick the Great landed on a novel strategy to keep money flowing into his borders. He organized cash-poor nobles into cooperatives, and began offering, to the highest bidders, bonds based on the value of their land. European investors snapped them up, giving Prussia the injection of cash it needed. It was, as the journalist Robin Wigglesworth writes in his new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic History of How Bonds Built the Modern World, possibly the world’s first mortgage bond sale. is a rollicking look at the development of the bond market, perhaps the least appreciated—but, Wigglesworth convincingly argues, the most important—financial market in the world today. Wigglesworth connects overzealous use of bonds both to the Great Recession and to America’s massive ballooning $40 trillion national debt. Paired with another recent book, David I. Backer’s As Public As Possible: Radical Finance for America’s Public Schools, which chronicles the crushing consequences of the bond market on public schools, a picture emerges of bonds as a little-noticed, and increasingly popular, lever for inequality.Whether we realize it or not, bonds interlace nearly every facet of our lives. They are basically IOUs that pay out on fixed terms, and that governments and other large institutions issue to raise money. If you have an investment portfolio, it probably contains a slice of bonds sold by the U.S. Treasury. The interest rates of Treasury bondstend to define the entire market: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates on its long-term bonds, as it did recently, your auto lender and your credit card company will probably soon hike their rates, too. But bonds show up in increasingly far-flung corners of the economy, too.Bonds likely fund your local public school or bridge improvement project, and they facilitate the resale of your home mortgage. Summer camps issue bonds to raise money, and so do hospitals and local, state, and national governments. All kinds of consumer debts can be repackaged as bonds, and sold to ever more distant bidders.

item.title: Leadership Dispatch: Filter or funnel
item.author: bounces+r8ummxv832soh3p8536c2hdx2548ds7h376k@ckespa.joshdoody.com
item.content:encoded: This week's Leadership Dispatch is about how to decide what news to share with your team and when to share it.​If you share every whiff of bad news with your team, they may become paranoid and paralyzed, preventing them from doing their work. But of course you need to share bad news sometimes.​And what about good news? Should you just share everything you can? Sharing unconfirmed rumors could be counter-productive, but you do get a boost when you share some good news.So how do you decide what to share and when to share it?Use the "Filter or funnel" framework to make those decisions easier and more strategic:One of the most challenging aspects of leadership is deciding what information to share with your team and when to share it. In general, you should over-communicate so everyone is on the same page as often as possible, but you shouldn’t communicate to your team.Here’s a rubric to help you decide what to communicate:You are privy to a lot more of your organization’s inner workings and machinations than your team is. And while you want them to be synced up, you don’t want them to be paranoid or possibly paralyzed by fear and uncertainty. You also don’t want them to be excited about something coming down the pike only for them to be disappointed when it doesn’t come to fruition.When thinking about filtering, your threshold for sharing potential bad news should be high.Here are some questions you might ask before sharing bad news with your team:If the bad news is confirmed or at least extremely likely and it will affect your team, then you might want to get out ahead of it. If they can help prevent the bad thing from happening or at least prepare better, then you might enlist them once they understand the stakes and how they can help.When thinking about , be generous. Once you confirm the good news, then lean toward sharing it unless it may be a distraction or might better be saved as a surprise. Sharing good news is a way to encourage your team, bolster morale, and counterbalance the daily frustrations that come along.

item.title: Searching for answers after a "disappointing" Royals season
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: The Royals held their annual wrap-up press conference on Wednesday. In a year where they expectation was playoffs and the reality was 69 wins, this was a grim autopsy on a season that manager Matt Quatraro said was “frustrating” and General Manager JJ Picollo termed “disappointing.” I would concur with both of those adjectives. Entering the season, expectations were high. It was obvious fairly early on that they wouldn't come close to meeting those expectations.As usual, I'll highlight some of the key moments from the press conference by quoting Picollo or Quatraro. Then, I'll add a little analysis for my take.We start with the news that broke on Tuesday that hitting coach Alec Zumwalt will not be in the Royals dugout next year. Funny…nobody really knows how to categorize what the Royals did with Zumwalt. He didn’t get reassigned necessarily. He is still the Senior Director of Hitting Performance. He just lost the title of Hitting Coach. His responsibilities have shifted? His duties have become more focused?Whatever happened, according to Picollo, the shift in focus to the minor leagues for Zumwalt was part of the long-term plan when he joined the major league staff.“This was something that was anticipated the day he was brought to the major leagues. He came up in the middle of ’22. Alec had a tremendous history with all of the guys that are most of the guys on our team, but the core that you all have seen play here for two or three years. So it was important to have him on the staff when we did, and he did a good job.”According to Picollo, Zumwalt leaving his hitting coach role in 2026 was part of the motivation behind adding Connor Dawson and Marcus Thames last year to the staff as hitting coaches along with Zumwalt. They serve as continuity as Zumwalt moves out of the dugout. And Picollo says the club will fill the spot Zumwalt is vacating. He anticipates that will be done sometime in October.Seems like a lot of dominios the front office was trying to align. According to Picollo, he and Zumwalt had the “is it time to return to the minors?” talk in the last couple of winters.“Alec and I had a conversation to end of every season about is this the time to go back to the minor leagues. So this is really about succession planning. And there was succession plans in place. And there's a lot of confidence in what Alec did as a minor league coordinator and even some of the things he did in the major leagues...And the truth of the matter, he's good. He's a good hitting coach.”You may disagree with Picollo’s assessment of Zumwalt and, honestly, I’m not sure where I land. I don’t think he’s as terrible as a segment of the fanbase would have you believe. But the results are the results and, as I showed yesterday, they haven’t been good enough.From what I could glean, Dawson and Thames will be co-leads, so to speak.“As we get deeper into this offseason with Connor and Marcus, we'll hear more about their ideas. As assistants, they don't get to make the final call. Now those two will work together, and we'll find out more about what changes they may want to make.”I had heard rumblings that the belief in the organization is that the improved offense over the season was due to Thames and Dawson making inroads with players. Building relationships takes time. If that was truly the case, the progress made was tangible.A co-lead position is an interesting alignment where you have to coaches with very different backgrounds having an equal say. I don’t think the Royals would do this if they didn’t already have a good working relationship. Maybe this is the case where you don't really need a lead so to speak, but a couple of different voices for players when they're searching to unlock something. Still, it seems like this could sideways if there isn’t rock-solid alignment. Worth a shot, I suppose. They had to do something.Picollo opened the presser noting that not only would Zumwalt not be returning to the dugout, but almost the entire major league medical staff—Head Athletic Trainer Kyle Turner, Assistant Athletic Trainer Chris DeLucia and Major League Rehab Coordinator Jeff Blum—would be leaving the club. Also moving to a minor league role is Melissa Lambert who was Director of Behaviorial Science.This feels pretty seismic. Turner had been with the Royals for 17 years. DeLucia was with the team for 20 years and Blum was here for 19 years. The trio had all been in their current positions for five seasons. Lambert is returning to a focus on the minor leagues after four seasons in her role in the dugout. She’s been with the team since 2020.Picollo on the cashiering of the major league medical staff:“The way to look at that, most of those injuries there you have an idea going into it that there's an indicator that somebody may not have 10 years left three years left whatever and there were some indicators with some of our pitchers. You just don't want it to all happen at once… We try to do our best to prevent injuries. I think what we want to move to is a little more efficient way of getting guys back on the field. We've had some guys that haven't had surgeries that missed a significant amount of time. This is where I think the different departments all have to work together.”I believe what Picollo is referring to about indicators is that pitcher injuries aren’t usually sudden. It’s something that teams are aware of where they try to manage the situation and milk as many innings out of their arms they can. And then there’s the rehab situation. Clearly, the Royals were not happy with the length of time some of these players needed to return to the field.The thing that really stuck with me about the injuries from the 2026 season was how it seemed as though the Royals often dithered when making the call whether or not to put a player on the IL. They often played short-handed due to their indecisiveness. It was odd.According to Sportrac, the Royals lost 1,796 days to the IL in 2026. That’s about the middle of the pack in the majors. For reference, though, the Royals lost just 994 days to the IL in 2024. Either way, in 2026 there were a lot of injuries and a lot of missed days.Picollo was asked about how the Royals will address the avoiding another slow start in 2027 like the one that doomed them this year. The Royals were 15 games under .500 and 11 games out of first place in the AL Central on May 31. The record was the culmination of a March and April where they went 12-19 and followed that up with a May where they were even worse at 10-18.“One thing I've thought about, and I know Q thinks about a lot, we come out of Arizona, which is a very offensive environment. So what's in your mind coming out is “hit”. And then the reality is you come here and it's cold. You go somewhere else and it's raining and sleeting. You don't have ideal conditions. But how do we combat that?…There's no magic formula for it. You just have to try to prepare. I do think, not just the Kansas City Royals, but I think there were several teams across baseball that were impacted by the WBC. We didn't have our team in spring training…We know all the players from the Royals that played. They did well. They were a national story. But when we got back together, it was like beginning of March again. But it was time to go. It was a regular season.”I get it. The ball jumps in Arizona in Spring Training. It’s quite a different environment when the regular season starts in Kansas City the last week of March. And they did have plenty of players at the World Baseball Classic. Except the above statement feels like thin gruel given that those issues were often the same for every single team in the league. And the supposed hangover from the WBC and the shift from Arizona to colder weather lasted for a long time. Two months!It just feels flimsy to point to those two things as factors in the team not performing up to expectations. I couldn't tell you why it happened, but I do know having your closer serve up a walkoff grand slam in the second game of the season followed by slow starts from several key offensive players followed by the buildup of injuries to the rotation and the general underperformance from the bullpen certainly seemed to snowball as the early weeks moved by. These sorts of things happen. Usually not all of them at once, but they happen. To point at having Spring Training in Arizona and the WBC as reasons seems a bit farfetched.An area of focus this winter will be the bullpen. Obviously. Picollo noted that the Royals have been in the top five in spending on their bullpen over the last three years. He also acknowledged that splashing the cash on relievers, who are naturally finicky, may not be the best use of resources.:“There's other ways to match up. And neutral relievers, neutral split relievers, left-on-left guys, guys that dominate right-handers, which is not usually the one you need the most of. There's different ways to do it, different arm slots. If you look at some of the acquisitions we had in the latter part of this year, we had some guys who were straight power, where we want to refine their command, and some guys are different arm slot guys. Let's see how that works for us.Now it's a matter of just trying to put it all together. There's not a clear definitive answer on how to put a bullpen together, but I think the variety of different looks, different stuff, type of relievers is the way we're probably going to go.”As for the closer, Picollo said they didn’t have anyone they were focused on for that role in 2027. They don’t think that they have one currently on the roster. I believe if it’s anyone, it’s Lucas Erceg. Especially if he can bottle those 100 mph fastballs. He was a completely different pitcher when he returned from Triple-A. Dare I say, closer-esque.As for the position players, Picollo said Jac Caglianone will stay in right field and Vinnie Pasquantino is the primary first baseman going forward. He said that a focus will be finding more production—and better defense from left and center field. Carson Roccaforte, coming off a 30/30 season between Double and Triple-A has earned a look in center. It kind of makes me wonder if they’ll tender a contract to Kyle Isbel. He earned $2.7 million in 2026 and is eligible for arbitration the for the third time. He doesn’t break the bank, but his offensive degraded to the point that his defense couldn’t compensate. And his defense took a step back due to his foot issues.The Royals lineup, as Picollo noted, is a bit left-handed heavy. They will be looking for balance. I kind of doubt they’d play the free agent market for a center fielder. Maybe Roccaforte has pushed his way to the front. For left field, there are a couple of right-handed hitters who will be available in the open market. Randy Arozarena is one, but he would command some dollars. Taylor Ward is another option, one that would be less expensive. He did well starting the season in Baltimore but then cratered after he was dealt to Seattle. Sliding down the scale, Ian Happ would be an even less expensive option. All three players are in their early 30s.A couple of quick hits to wrap:After opening the season with nine pitchers they felt could slot into the starting rotation and finishing the year with just three of those guys healthy, Picollo will never take starting pitching depth for granted.Daniel Lynch IV has earned the opportunity to compete for a role in the rotation.Picollo expects the Royals will pick up the option on Tony Gonsolin.It doesn’t sound as if the Royals will be talking contract extensions with Jac Caglianone and Carter Jensen this winter. They’ll wait until they have two full years of service time before they open those talks.Picollo is open to making trades to add to the roster, but he’s looking for major league talent. Not prospects. The goal is to win now.Overall, a typical end of the season wrap from Picollo and Quatraro. I realize I didn't pull any Q quotes but he said a few things that I'll look into a little deeper in the coming days. Otherwise, it feels like the focus is on the right things going forward in addressing the injuries and rehab time to get players back on the field, along with shuffling the hitting coaches. The upcoming lockout will also play a factor in how the Royals move once the postseason wraps up. This is a pivotal offseason for the Royals. After the shortcomings in 2025 and the absolute failure of 2026, they have to get it right for 2027.
