item.title: Andros Fenollosa: How I built a WhatsApp client for Emacs without an API
item.author: Andros Fenollosa
item.content:encoded: One of the most fun things you can do with Emacs is to build an interface for another piece of software. It is the Lisp version of running Doom on any device. It is also quite useful, because you can connect it to other tools in the gnu's editor and build more pleasant workflows.The big question: can I chat on WhatsApp from Emacs? Spoiler: I made it, with some limitations.Context: I work on macOS. It matters, because the solution depends on it.Meta offers no API for this, and the macOS desktop app has no bridge at all: no open ports, no gRPC, no AppleScript dictionary. Nothing.There are unofficial clients, like whatsmeow, that talk directly to WhatsApp's servers by pretending to be a device. They work, but your account ends up depending on software Meta does not authorize, and it is one more process to maintain. On top of that, Meta can detect them and ban your number. I am not going to risk my account just to chat from Emacs.So how do you talk to an app that does not want to talk to you? By reading the same thing it reads.The WhatsApp app stores every chat in a local SQLite file:~/Library/Group Containers/group.net.whatsapp.WhatsApp.shared/ChatStorage.sqliteEmacs 29 ships with SQLite built in, no external libraries. Opening it read-only takes one line:The schema is undocumented, so I had to explore it by hand. Chats live in , messages in , and group member names in and . That at the start of every name gives it away: it is a Core Data database.And Core Data has a surprise. Dates do not count from 1970, but from . My first messages showed up dated 1995. The fix: a constant.(defconst whatsapp--epoch-offset 978307200 "Seconds between the Unix epoch and the Core Data epoch (2001-01-01).")There were more traps. Pinned chats store a date in the future so they stay on top, and the text of the session's last message is encoded. Better to read both from the message itself.One more detail: macOS protects that directory. You have to give Emacs in the privacy settings. I would hand Emacs the keys to my house if it asked.Sending: the Shortcuts trickReading is easy. What about writing? Editing the database is pointless: the app would not notice and nothing would go out over the network.Then I remembered that the WhatsApp app provides an action in macOS : "Send Message". And Shortcuts can be run from the terminal:shortcuts run "Send WhatsApp" --input-path message.jsonThe problem is that the action expects a contact from your address book, not a number. The trick: build a with the chat's phone number, which the shortcut turns into a temporary contact. Nothing is saved in your address book.Emacs writes a JSON file with the vCard and the text, starts the process and waits:(json-encode `((vcard . ,(whatsapp--vcard name phone)) (text . ,text)))The full flow looks like this:flowchart LR E[Emacs] -- reads --> DB[(ChatStorage.sqlite)] E -- JSON with vCard --> S[Send WhatsApp shortcut] S -- Send Message --> W[Official WhatsApp app] W -- stores --> DBI like one detail. While the shortcut runs, the message shows as . When WhatsApp stores it in its database, Emacs replaces it with the real one. What you see is what WhatsApp actually sent, not what Emacs thinks it sent.An ERC or rcirc style interface, with a chat list and one buffer per conversation:--- Wednesday 1 October 2026 --- [08:15] <Alice> Good morning! [08:16] <Me> Morning! Are we still on for today? [08:20] <Alice> Yes, 10:00 at the station [08:21] <Alice> [image] This is the entrance Alice> _This is the most trivial part of the whole thing. Emacs solved this problem decades ago.The whole client fits in a few lines of Elisp, with no dependencies.It has its limits, of course.You cannot write to groups, because the Shortcuts action only accepts people.Some chats do not store the phone number locally and stay read-only.And there are no notifications: you press to fetch new messages.But now I can talk to my family without leaving Emacs. What more could you ask for?Help me keep writing Every coffee gives me a push toward the next article. Sure, it's on me!

item.title: TKB (Guest rec from Ryan Mandelbaum)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we have a guest recommendation from , a writer and occasional DJ, whose newsletter is a valuable source of thoughtful curation and honest reflections on the world of experimental sound.Today I’d like to shine a light on an artist who is, in my opinion, one of the most brilliant and overlooked minds currently operating in the world of ambient and experimental adjacent sound, someone I recommend whenever I am given the chance: Timothy K. Brown aka TKB.Trying to describe TKB’s sound in terms of musical reference points is nearly impossible because, simply put, there is nothing out there quite like it. It is a sound that I’d best describe as elemental – as if he somehow discovered a method for recording the ancient music of the earth itself, the essential and imperceptible melody that vibrates through everyone and everything. TKB’s entire discography is well worth delving into, but his three most recent releases (each respectively finding their way to the very top of my year end lists) are all perfect launching points.is an otherworldly and at times disorienting listen filled with some of the most unique textures I’ve ever heard. Jon Hassell, Zoviet France, and even the work of James Ferraro and Spencer Clarke are the closest comparisons I can think of, but again… TKB’s world is entirely his own. released just a few months later on World of Knots, takes a much more rhythmic approach, its exoskeletal rhythmic patterns far removed from any sense human involvement, rather resembling those found in nature – the fluttering of moth wings, the whisper of wind through leaves, the mating call of crickets dancing in and out of phase with each other.is easily TKB’s most serene work yet. While it might be absent of the jittery and at times anxious sense of constant motion present in much of his work, it is nonetheless defined by the same sense of dark mystery, as if one is peering into the very deepest part of the night, and given access to its most forbidden secrets. Don’t let this description scare you off though – this is possibly the most beautiful album of the year, perfect to drift off to. A much needed corner of serenity in a constantly overstimulating world.

item.title: Forgotten Band: The Damned
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There is a strange little corner of rock history occupied by bands that were important enough to change music but somehow never became household names. The Damned sit comfortably in that category.If you know punk, you know The Damned. If you know British rock history, you probably know The Damned. If you have ever gone down a rabbit hole involving punk, goth, post-punk, garage rock, or alternative music, you’ve almost certainly encountered them.But ask the average person to name the most important British punk bands and you’re likely to hear the Sex Pistols, The Clash, and perhaps The Buzzcocks. The Damned might eventually appear somewhere down the list.That is remarkable because The Damned were there from the very beginning.They were not merely observers of the original British punk explosion. They were one of the bands responsible for creating it.They were the first British punk band to release a single. They released one of the first British punk albums. They played fast, loud, obnoxious music before most of the country had even figured out what punk was supposed to sound like.And then, rather than spending the rest of their career making the same record over and over, they started changing.They became darker. Stranger. More theatrical. More melodic. More psychedelic. More gothic. At various points they sounded like a punk band, a garage band, a goth band, a psychedelic rock group, and a completely unhinged rock ‘n’ roll circus.That refusal to stay in one box may have been part of the reason they never became as commercially recognizable as some of their contemporaries.It is also exactly what makes The Damned so interesting.The Damned emerged in London during the mid-1970s, when the British music scene was beginning to fracture.Progressive rock had become increasingly elaborate. Arena rock was getting bigger and more polished. Glam had provided an explosion of theatricality, but even that movement was becoming part of the established music business.Meanwhile, a collection of young musicians were discovering that you didn’t need enormous budgets, virtuoso musicianship, or twenty-minute songs to make something exciting.The original Damned lineup featured Dave Vanian on vocals, Captain Sensible on guitar, Rat Scabies on drums, and Brian James on guitar. It was an unlikely combination of personalities, but together they created something that was immediate and confrontational.Dave Vanian looked like he had wandered out of a horror movie.Captain Sensible looked like he might have wandered in from an entirely different one.And the music sounded like somebody had plugged a jet engine into a Marshall amplifier.The Damned were not interested in sounding respectable.New Rose Changes EverythingIn October 1976, The Damned released “New Rose.”It is difficult to overstate the historical importance of that record.“New Rose” is widely recognized as the first single released by a British punk band.The Sex Pistols were generating enormous controversy. The Clash were beginning to develop their identity. The Buzzcocks were emerging from Manchester.But The Damned got their record out first.And they didn’t ease anybody into the new musical landscape.“New Rose” was short, aggressive, fast, and completely uninterested in traditional rock-radio conventions.It sounded like a band trying to kick down the door.The single immediately established something that would become a recurring theme throughout The Damned’s career: they were capable of being ridiculous and dangerous at exactly the same time.There was humor underneath the aggression.There was theatricality underneath the speed.And there was a genuine love of old-fashioned rock ‘n’ roll underneath all the noise.That combination would become one of their defining characteristics.In February 1977, The Damned released .The album was produced by Nick Lowe and became one of the foundational records of British punk.It was also incredibly short.The entire thing moves like somebody has just announced that the building is on fire.There isn’t much interest in wasting time.Songs arrive, explode, and disappear before you’ve had time to get comfortable.The album contains some of the band’s best-known early material, including “Neat Neat Neat” and “New Rose,” but what makes the record important is its sense of urgency.The Damned weren’t trying to construct elaborate arrangements.They weren’t interested in proving how technically sophisticated they were.They wanted the songs to hit.The album helped establish the template for British punk’s first wave: short songs, loud guitars, furious drumming, memorable hooks, and an attitude that suggested the entire music industry could probably survive without them.The irony is that the music industry eventually couldn’t ignore them.The Band That Wouldn’t BehaveThe Damned quickly developed a reputation for chaos.That reputation wasn’t entirely accidental.Captain Sensible was one of the more colorful personalities in British punk. Dave Vanian brought a theatrical, almost gothic presence to the band. Rat Scabies was a ferocious drummer. Brian James brought a darker, more traditional punk-rock guitar sound.They didn’t necessarily look like a conventional rock band.They didn’t act like one either.And they certainly didn’t sound like one for very long.After their first album, Brian James departed following internal tensions and disagreements.Instead of collapsing, The Damned began moving in a completely different direction.This is where their story gets particularly interesting.Most punk bands faced a basic choice: continue making increasingly polished versions of their original sound or evolve into something else.The Damned chose option three.They seemed determined to see how many different musical identities they could cram into one career.The band’s second album, , arrived in 1977.It was not received as enthusiastically as the debut.Part of the problem was that it was already showing signs that The Damned weren’t interested in simply repeating themselves.Captain Sensible was increasingly involved in the band’s musical direction, and their sound was becoming more experimental.The Damned eventually broke up.For most bands, that would have been the end.For The Damned, it was more like an intermission.They returned in the late 1970s with a different sound and a significantly different atmosphere.The punk fury was still there, but it was being replaced by something more sinister.Something more atmospheric.Something that would help lay groundwork for gothic rock.Then came in 1979.This is where the argument for The Damned’s importance becomes almost impossible to ignore.The album contains punk, garage rock, psychedelic influences, pop hooks, and the beginnings of the darker sound that would become associated with goth.“Love Song” showed that The Damned could write something catchy without losing their edge.“Smash It Up” demonstrated their ability to turn punk aggression into something almost celebratory.And “Plan 9 Channel 7” leaned heavily into the band’s fascination with horror, atmosphere, and 1960s garage rock.The Damned were becoming something much bigger than a punk band.They were becoming a strange hybrid of everything they liked.That was one of their greatest strengths.They weren’t embarrassed to love pop music.They weren’t embarrassed to love horror movies.They weren’t embarrassed to love psychedelic rock.They weren’t embarrassed to love garage rock.And they certainly weren’t embarrassed to make fun of themselves.If The Damned are remembered for anything beyond punk, it is their influence on gothic rock.Dave Vanian’s appearance had already given the band a visual identity unlike most of their punk contemporaries.With his pale makeup, dark clothing, and theatrical presentation, Vanian looked less like a punk singer and more like a rock-and-roll vampire.And then there was the music.The band’s next major phase would push further into dark, atmospheric territory., released in 1980, demonstrated just how far they had traveled from the frantic three-chord assault of .The album included lengthy, atmospheric material alongside more conventional songs.It wasn’t simply punk anymore.The Damned were becoming one of those bands where the label started getting in the way.Calling them punk was accurate.Calling them goth was also reasonable.Calling them rock was obvious.Calling them weird was probably the most accurate description of all.“Eloise” and the Commercial PeakThe Damned’s career took another unexpected turn in the mid-1980s.They scored one of their biggest commercial successes with their cover of “Eloise.”The song was dramatically different from the stripped-down punk of their early years.The arrangement was theatrical and bombastic, while Vanian’s voice gave the song an appropriately dramatic quality.The single became a major British hit and demonstrated that The Damned could operate within a much larger musical world than the punk scene that had originally produced them.But by then the band’s history had become a revolving door of personnel changes, breakups, reunions, and different musical directions.Captain Sensible had departed for a successful solo career.Vanian remained the central figure.And The Damned continued.That word may be the most important one in their entire story.The Captain Sensible ProblemOne reason The Damned’s history can be difficult for casual listeners to follow is that Captain Sensible became successful outside the band.His solo career produced the massive novelty hit “Happy Talk” in 1982, which reached number one in the United Kingdom.That song could hardly have been further removed from the image of The Damned.This was the same Captain Sensible who had helped create some of the most aggressive British punk music of the 1970s.Suddenly he was wearing a giant red beret and appearing on mainstream television.It was also completely consistent with his personality.Captain Sensible had never seemed particularly interested in following the rules of what a punk musician was supposed to be.The success of his solo career also contributed to the increasingly unusual trajectory of The Damned.They were no longer simply one band following one musical path.They were a collection of personalities constantly pulling the group in different directions.Somehow, they kept coming back together.Why Didn’t They Become as Famous as The Clash?This is the question that hangs over The Damned.Why aren’t they generally mentioned alongside The Clash and the Sex Pistols when discussing the defining British punk bands?There isn’t one simple answer.The Sex Pistols became cultural lightning rods.The Clash developed into one of the most politically significant rock bands of their era.The Damned were different.They didn’t have a single ideological message that defined them.They didn’t build their identity around political confrontation.They didn’t become the voice of a particular movement.They were more interested in music itself.They were also inconsistent in a way that made them fascinating but perhaps harder to market.A listener could discover The Damned through punk, goth, garage rock, alternative music, or even mainstream British pop.The band’s catalog didn’t have one obvious identity.And commercially, they never maintained the sustained success required to become one of the biggest bands of their generation.But that doesn’t mean they weren’t influential.In fact, their influence may be easier to hear in other bands than in their own record sales.The Forgotten Link Between Punk and GothThe Damned occupy a fascinating position in British music.They were part of the original punk explosion, but their willingness to experiment helped point toward the darker alternative music that followed.That makes them an important bridge between several movements.You can hear elements of punk’s speed and aggression.You can hear garage rock.You can hear psychedelic rock.You can hear horror-film imagery.You can hear the beginnings of gothic rock.You can hear pop songwriting.You can even hear the seeds of the alternative rock that would become much more prominent in the 1980s and 1990s.They weren’t necessarily inventing each of those things independently.Their importance comes from combining them.The Damned essentially treated genres as suggestions rather than rules.A Band That Refused to Grow UpThere is also something wonderfully strange about The Damned’s longevity.Many punk bands eventually became serious.The Damned never entirely did.It may have been their secret weapon.There was always a sense that they understood rock music was supposed to be fun.Even when the music became darker, there was still humor underneath it.Even when the band became more theatrical, there was still punk aggression.Even when they experimented, they never completely abandoned the simple pleasure of turning up the volume and making a lot of noise.That attitude allowed them to survive changes in musical fashion that destroyed plenty of other bands.Post-punk became new wave.New wave became goth and alternative rock.The 1980s became the 1990s.Alternative rock became mainstream.And The Damned were still around.The easiest way to understand The Damned’s legacy is to stop looking for one particular sound.They weren’t important because they created a single genre.They were important because they demonstrated how much freedom a rock band could have.A band could be punk and melodic.It could be aggressive and funny.It could be dark without taking itself too seriously.It could move from two-minute punk songs to extended psychedelic pieces.It could wear horror-movie imagery without becoming a novelty act.And it could change without completely losing its identity.That is a difficult trick.Most bands that change dramatically eventually sound like different bands.The Damned often sounded like The Damned even when the music around them was completely different.So, Are The Damned Really Forgotten?Among punk fans, they are anything but forgotten.Among musicians, their influence is obvious.Among people who know British alternative music, their name carries considerable weight.But compared with the fame of The Clash, the Sex Pistols, or even later bands influenced by them, The Damned remain strangely underappreciated by the wider public.And perhaps that is the great irony of their career.They were one of the first British punk bands to put a record on the shelves.They released one of the most important early punk albums.They helped establish the sound and attitude of British punk.They helped point toward gothic rock.They produced some genuinely great rock songs.They survived numerous personnel changes and breakups.They continued recording and performing decades after the original punk explosion.And yet they somehow remain the band people discover after they have already discovered everybody else.Maybe that is actually the best way to discover The Damned.Start with the obvious names.Listen to the Sex Pistols.Then eventually someone mentions The Damned.You put on expecting another historical punk artifact.Instead, you discover a band that sounds alive.Then you hear and realize they’re doing something completely different.Then you hear .Then you find the gothic material.Then Captain Sensible’s solo work.Suddenly the supposedly “forgotten” band has turned into a rabbit hole.And that’s probably the most appropriate fate for The Damned.They were never particularly good at staying where people expected them to stay.Why should their place in rock history be any different?The Damned weren’t simply one of the first British punk bands.They were one of the bands that proved punk could become almost anything.The fact that they never became as famous as some of their contemporaries doesn’t make their story less important.If anything, it makes rediscovering them more rewarding.The Damned weren’t forgotten because they weren’t important.They were forgotten because rock history has a bad habit of simplifying itself.Punk becomes three bands.Goth becomes another handful.Alternative rock gets its own list.Garage rock gets another.The messy connections between all of them disappear.The Damned don’t fit neatly into any of those boxes.They belong in all of them.And that’s exactly why, more than four decades after their debut, The Damned still sound like a band waiting to be rediscovered.

item.title: Raymond Zeitler: Now org-toggle-timestamp-overlays is Disabled
item.author: Raymond Zeitler
item.content:encoded:
The default keybinding of is . Today I learned about another command with a similar keybinding () -- org-toggle-timestamp-overlays. Note the in the middle.
When I pressed that key combination (inadvertently), all the YYYY-MM-DD timestamps in the buffer were converted to the MM/DD/YYYY format. This was unacceptable -- I needed to change them back. However did not revert the timestamps; it just undid the last edit. Furthermore, these undesired timestamps couldn't be edited and were impervious to . I was confused yet again.
I didn't even know how this happened. So I invoked as a kind reader once suggested and discovered org-toggle-timestamp-overlays.
The docstring was no help – it's self-evident that it would "Toggle the use of custom time stamp formats." Eager to clock out of my task, I didn't care to learn more. All I wanted to do was undo the effect.
I figured that since it toggles the timestamp, all I had to do was invoke it again to toggle it back. Nope. Well, a nice message appears, saying "Time stamp overlays removed." Yet the timestamps looked the same.
Undaunted, I figured I'd reload the buffer with . That had no effect. To finally fix this, I deleted the buffer and revisited the file.
A command like this surely is in the same category as , which is disabled by default. And so this is why I added (put 'org-toggle-timestamp-overlays 'disabled t) to my init file.

item.title: Rahul Juliato: Readable Regular Expressions for JavaScript/TypeScript, Inspired by Emacs' rx
item.author: Rahul Juliato
item.content:encoded: Quick, what does this match?That's the official regexp from semver.org. It validates version numbers like:Don't get me wrong, I love regexps, but in practice you probably spend a bunch of time writing one, testing it against some cases, and moving on, proud of your achievement!Some time passes and lucky future you (or unlucky someone else) has to change it. Dramatic pause here.I bet you've been there. Now your options are probably: decode it again from the start, rewrite the whole thing, or, in the age of AI, ask (and hopefully not blindly accept) an LLM for a new recipe.Emacs has had a nice answer for more readable regexps for a long time: the macro. I started using it all the time in Emacs Lisp, as reviewers always suggested it to me. Later, I started missing this DSL in JavaScript and TypeScript, so I wrote a small version of it for my projects.So, what about reading that SemVer regexp like in the code below?The same strings match, and you get named groups as a bonus. By the end of this post you'll know every piece of it. the here has nothing to do with RxJS, which is an amazing library for reactive programming with observables.A taste of rx in Emacs LispWith you describe a regexp as a tree of named forms, and Emacs turns it into the regexp string for you: means a parenthesis. You don't need to escape anything by hand. Every form takes a list of things and matches them one after the other. You don't need to wrap them in a , even though exists.Groups appear only when needed. becomes , not .The proposed JavaScript/TypeScript version in this post reads like this:If you want strings to be literals, you can't represent a regexp piece as a plain , otherwise you can't tell (a literal parenthesis) apart from (a group you built). So every piece is a small object: is the regexp text. records how that text behaves when you glue it to other things:: a single unit, like , , or . You can put a quantifier right after it.: safe to concatenate, but a quantifier needs around it. is a , and so is , since would silently turn into a lazy quantifier.: has a at the top level, so it needs almost everywhere.Plain strings go through , which escapes them:With that in place, joins nodes and only brackets alternations:(That backreference check is one of those bugs you only find by writing tests, or when it happens to you in prod. followed by the literal gives you backreference number ten.)Every quantifier is a of its arguments plus a suffix, bracketed only when the body isn't an atom:Because each quantifier calls on its arguments, you get the implicit sequence for free: becomes .And finally, the two entry points. As in Emacs, returns a string. returns a you can use right away: exists because Emacs controls case folding through the variable, and JavaScript puts it on the regexp itself.That's the whole engine! Now, let's build our vocabulary.In Emacs you write . Inside those strings, is a range, and a at either end is a plain dash. I kept the same rule:The dash comes out escaped because sets can merge. If you combine with , an unescaped would end up in the middle and create a range from to . Escaping it costs one backslash.And merging is the reason why has a field. It is there to hold the text that goes between and , so can take other sets as arguments: negates a set, and it knows the shorthand classes:The simple email check, which most of us have written as /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/ at some point, becomes:The rest of the Emacs character classes are there too: , , , , , , , , , , , , , , and . One difference: in Emacs they understand Unicode, and mine are ASCII only. won't match .Two more come from rx's symbol list, and people (me, many times) mix them up:In rx, really means anything, newlines included. Here is where the difference shows up:Alternatives, and the longest match works as you'd expect, and gets bracketed when it lands inside a sequence:Did you notice the order changed? I copied that behavior from Emacs. When every branch of an is a plain string, rx hands them to , which builds a pattern that prefers the longest match:JavaScript alternation takes the first branch that matches, going left to right. So the naive regexp for a list of keywords has a 'bug':I don't build a trie like does. Sorting the strings by length, longest first, is enough to get the same behavior:As in Emacs, with no branches returns , which is here. It's handy when you build the branch list at runtime and it might come out empty.Repetition, greedy and lazyEmacs has , and . Here they are , and :The lazy versions , and are , and . The classic HTML tag example:Groups and backreferences is a capturing group, and points back to it:Emacs also has to pick the group number. JavaScript can't do that, but it has named groups, which serve the same purpose and read better: accepts a name as well: distinguishes the start of the string () from the start of a line (). In JavaScript both are , and the flag decides which one you get. I kept both names so the intent shows in the code:Why not add and automatically? Because you only want them when validating a whole string. When searching inside a text, as in , or , a hidden and would break everything. Emacs agrees: and are explicit in too. and map straight to and . Emacs also has and ( and ), start and end of a word. JavaScript lacks those, so I combined with a lookaround:Plain strings are already literals, but has an explicit form for strings computed at runtime, and I kept it. It documents that the value came from somewhere else:The opposite direction is 's form, the escape hatch. Here it's , and it receives either a string or an existing . It lets you adopt the DSL in a codebase full of old regexps without rewriting all of them, like: can't see inside the text it gets, so it adds brackets whenever it's combined with something else. It's an extra , and the regexp still works.Shall we try SemVer again?Back to the regexp from the intro. In Emacs you would give names to the pieces with or . In TypeScript those are just s:Now you can read the spec in the code. A numeric identifier is , or a non-zero digit followed by any number of digits. A pre-release is a dotted list of identifiers, and so is build metadata. is a plain function returning a node, which is as far as abstraction needs to go here.It matches the same strings as the official regexp, and the named groups give you a result like:Next time the spec changes, you can understand what the current regex does at a glance, instead of fighting an army of punctuation.What's missing from Emacs rxI tried to map every form, and a few have no JavaScript equivalent:: JavaScript regexps don't know about a cursor., , , : these depend on Emacs syntax tables.: possible with the flag, but I haven't needed it. / : these flip the greediness of everything inside them. Doable, but it would need a separate pass, and the functions cover my use cases.: TypeScript already evaluates expressions everywhere, so you get it for free.And one addition Emacs doesn't need: ., implicit in every form, , , , , , (with the flag), Examples: JS/TS regex vs RXEach example below shows the goal, the Emacs form in a comment, the regexp you would write by hand, and the version. When produces a different regexp text, the line shows it. The results at the bottom come from running both against the same strings.The whole string is digits.The whole string is ASCII letters.Both spellings, color and colour.Two words separated by a space.(123) 456-7890, parentheses and all.An optional sign, then digits.A string without any digit.Exactly three comma-separated fields. or , then a name, keeping the title.Three or more digits, anywhere.An open tag and its own closing tag. as a word, not inside another one.It's a single file with no dependencies. Copy it into your project and start deleting the forms you don't need, or adding the ones you miss.You can check the same code, plus all the examples from this post (and a few more), in this gist. If you'd rather not set anything up, paste it into the TypeScript Playground, hit "Run", and check the "Logs" tab.None of this is new. On the Emacs side, as I said before, has shipped for decades, and the Elisp version is more complete than mine.The idea of describing patterns with a small DSL instead of raw syntax isn't new either. Plenty of people have tried it, each in their own way. One project I like a lot in this space is Zod, which I wrote about in my Zod quick tutorial. It's not a regexp builder: you compose small schema pieces, and Zod gives you back a parser and a TypeScript type from the same construction. It follows the same spirit, though: build big things out of small named pieces you can read.If you write Elisp and have never tried , open , type , and it. If you write JavaScript or TypeScript, the file above is yours. And if you port it to another language, send me a link.

item.title: Doubts About the AI Boom Are Seeping Into Elite Headlines
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: This is the weekly, free edition of The Backchannel. If you’d like to receive the free edition of The Backchannel in your inbox, you can subscribe here. In my recent writing about LLMs and AI, I’ve mainly focused on what it can do, what it is, what its potential dangers are. I haven’t focused as much on the pretty substantial evidence that we’re in the midst of an AI bubble. The entire U.S. economy is heavily dependent on the AI boom. Much of the rest of the economy is in a slump. That boom is based on cheap money and very high expectations for AI profits, just as the Fed is facing irresistible pressure to raise interest rates, which is to say, raise the cost of money. This whole question of an AI bubble gets talked about a lot. You probably know the basic outlines. What’s caught my attention is how just in the last week or so these questions, verging into assumptions about unsustainable spending, are bleeding into the tech and the Beltway political press.

item.title: Appeals Courts Slowly Awaken to Trump II Threat
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Two Steps Forward, One Step BackIn the defining legal struggle of our time — whether the federal judiciary will sustain the rule of law long enough to preserve the essential core of a democracy for us to repair, rebuild, and re-enlarge after Trump II — the jury is still out.Important developments in three different cases yesterday — the Alien Enemies Act, third-country deportations, and Trump’s collusive settlement with the IRS — point in very different directions.On the face of it, not much unites the cases or offers a common theme or collective takeaway. But in stepping back and reviewing the last 20 months of Trump II legal battles, yesterday’s developments are datapoints in favor of a tentative working theory that appeals courts are slowly coming around to the urgency of the current moment.In the first six months of Trump II, district judges were on their heels, caught off guard by the ferocity of the rampage against the rule of law and still tethered to old norms and expectations for the Justice Department that no longer held true. It was a brutal stretch of watching the Trump administration seize some key early wins and capture important legal ground.After being collectively kicked in the teeth, district judges pretty quickly adjusted to the new reality — but appeals courts failed to back district judges in key respects, missed the urgency of the moment, and surrendered more ground to the lawlessness.More recently, appellate judges have begun to turn, too. Two glimmers of hope yesterday came at the appeals court level, with the en banc D.C. Circuit looking poised to allow U.S. District Judge James Boasberg to resume his contempt of court inquiry in the original Alien Enemies Act case and the 11th Circuit handing Trump a loss in his bogus settlement with the IRS.That still leaves the Supreme Court, which — with a few notable exceptions — has been Trump’s greatest enabler. It played true to form yesterday with an emergency intervention that will allow the administration’s brutal third-country removals policy to continue past the election and until it rules after oral arguments in December.Unlike the lower courts, the Supreme Court will not eventually come around. While we’ve already seen examples — most prominently on tariffs, birthright citizenship, and the USPS mail-in ballots rule — of the Roberts Court refusing to endorse some of Trump’s worst excesses, the high court is too deeply compromised and its six-justice right-wing majority too invested in the GOP’s partisan fate to emerge as a reliable bulwark.But the appeals courts may buy us some additional time by slowing the speed of the descent.A quick rundown on yesterday’s developments, in turn:AEA Contempt Inquiry Likely to ResumeThe 7-4 Democratic-Republican split on the en banc D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals already boded well for the prospect of Judge Boasberg being able to resume his inquiry into whether Trump administration officials, including DOJ lawyers, should be held in contempt of court for violating his orders to stop and turn around deportation flights under the Alien Enemies Act.Oral arguments left the strong impression that a majority of the full court will greenlight Boasberg’s inquiry. I’d pay particular attention to Judge Karen Henderson, a Bush I appointee who authored an important ruling on the substance of the Alien Enemies Act last year in the same case.For more, I wrote at some length about yesterday’s oral arguments here.Trump Takes a Loss in IRS CaseA unanimous three-judge panel of the 11th Circuit declined to put on hold the sanctions order by U.S. District Judge Kathleen M. Williams in Trump’s collusive lawsuit against the IRS.The ruling was made on procedural grounds, including that the appeal was premature given Williams hadn’t yet decided on the amount of attorney fees award in the case. But while the appeals court panel — two Obama appointees and one Trump appointee — didn’t reach the merits of Williams’ ruling it did conclude: “Given the record before us, the appellants have not made a strong showing that the district court committed clear error in its collusion and bad faith findings.”Roberts Courts Does It AgainThe Supreme Court intervened on an emergency basis to block lower court orders that had effectively frozen the Trump administration policy of deporting people without notice or hearing to countries they are not from and to which they have no connection.The three Democratic appointees opposed granting the stay.The decision by a federal court in Boston, and upheld by the 1st Circuit Court of Appeals, had required giving detainees a chance to voice fear of torture or persecution before being deported to third countries. Now the third-country deportations can resume with abandon.In what legal experts called an unusual twist, the Supreme Court identified three questions it wants briefed in the case, then gave the Trump administration the chance to identify any other issues it wants addressed: “Such other questions that the Government determines are appropriate for the proper disposition of the case.”The court fast-tracked oral arguments for December.Victim of ICE Shooting Charged in TexasWilber Rafael Garcés Perez, the Venezuelan national shot by an ICE agent in Austin, Texas 10 days ago, has been charged with assaulting a federal officer during their initial encounter.Garcés Perez, who was shot in the shoulder and still has a bullet in his back, allegedly hit the ICE agent with his vehicle’s side mirror as he fled the initial traffic stop. That portion of the incident is caught on the body cam of one of the officers, according to a court filing.Two observations about the filings:The shooting came a few moments later, after an alleged high-speed chase, when only one officer — without a body cam running — was present.In the court filing, a Homeland Security Investigations agent said he interviewed Garces Perez and the non-shooting agent after the incident, but gave no indication that he had interviewed the agent who fired his gun.Swimming in SchadenfreudeThe only proper way to cover the trio of Jack Smith hearings before Congress over the past year is as perjury trap under a veneer of disinformation — which is what made Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-MO) getting snared in his own perjury trap such a feast of mockery and memes.If you still haven’t gotten enough:TPM’s Hunter Walker: New Evidence Shows Just How Badly One Republican Senator Beclowned Himself in the Jack Smith HearingTPM’s John Light: 5 Points About a Senator’s Disastrous But Hilarious Attempt to Accuse Jack Smith of PerjuryCBP Funds Used for Pro-Trump TV AdsThe federal funds used to pay for pro-Trump TV ads airing in the stretch run of the midterm elections came from Customs and Border Protection, the WSJ reports. Outside monitors estimate some $1.4 million has been spent on the ads that have aired so far, but Democratic lawmakers claim allege that $20 million of CBP money has been shifted to the ad campaign.Two important and deeply corrosive moves by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to politicize the military and erode its professionalism:Hegseth is expected to announce today that he is cutting the number of flag officers by at least 20%. As with other Trump administration purges, the initial purge is usually only half of the equation. It’s who ultimately gets elevated in their place that cements the role of loyalists, hacks, and charlatans.23 Years Later, The U.S. Leaves IraqAfter more than two decades of unimaginable human carnage and sunk costs in toil and treasure, the last remaining U.S. forces in Iraq are departing the country today.

item.title: Irreal: Remember Remember Mode?
item.author: Irreal
item.content:encoded:
Over at the Emacs subreddit, BBSnek writes about discovering remember mode. It’s been around for a long time. I remember using it before Org mode. Indeed, I still use + to invoke because that was what I was used to with remember-mode.
Although I’m sure there are some, I can’t think of any reason to use remember-mode these days. Org mode can do everything it can and more. Org’s templates make capturing data and notes so much easier and, of course, you can bring all the other Org tools to bear on the results.
BBSnek uses it for quick notes—and it’s great for that—but Org can do that too and so much more. The truth is, I’m surprised that anyone is still using it for any other reason than inertia. Still, as usual, Emacs lets us have it our way and for those who prefer the simpler and lighter weight remember-mode, it’s there for them.

item.title: Are you smarter than the White House’s new AI chatbot? Let’s find out.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Oh, look — just what no one wanted, needed, or asked for.At a time when the rest of the world has fallen completely out of love with the idea of letting six-fingered plagiarism robots run wild, here comes the White House, to inflict on us its very own AI chatbot.“Well, we’re doing one thing. We’re gonna be signing a document at about five o’clock today, and— RENAMING— artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial. We all agree on that, and we’re gonna be naming it Super Intelligence. Officially renaming it.”This fucking idiot and his infantile obsession with renaming everything. Well listen up, everyone. I have an announcement to make, too. I’m also gonna be signing my own document today. I’m going to be officially renaming Donny to President Pants-Shitting Moron.It has a nice ring to it, doesn’t it?You know what? We should let the White House’s brand-spanking-new plagiarism robot fact-check that for us. I don’t answer political commentary or personal insults.If you have a question about a U.S. government service, benefit, or official process, I can help with that.What do you mean, you won’t respond to personal insults? That’s pretty fucking ironic, given whose White House this is coming from.I can’t help with insults or comments about anyone’s appearance.If you have a question about a U.S. government service, benefit, or official information, ask that and I’ll help.Fine, be that way. If you won’t explain what the hell is going on with Dear Leader’s fat, waterlogged head, maybe you’ll confirm a simple fact. Is Donny an adjudicated rapist?I don’t answer political commentary or legal conclusions about public figures.If you have a question about a U.S. government service, benefit, or official process, ask that and I’ll help.I only answer questions about U.S. government services and official information.If you have a question about a federal program, benefit, or process, ask that and I can help.Fuck you, Chatbot. You had the perfect opportunity to respond with, ‘an African or European swallow?’ — and you blew it. Who programmed you?The average cruising airspeed velocity of an unladen European swallow is roughly 11 meters per second, or 24 miles per hour (39 km/h). style.org +1The Reference: This famous question comes from the comedy film Monty Python and the Holy Grail, where the Bridgekeeper asks King Arthur about the speed of both European and African swallows • (which are non-migratory and cannot carry coconuts). (E) Interesting Engineering +4Check and mate, White House Chatbot. Get the fuck out of here.How out-of-touch and tone-deaf are these Donnyverse fucknuggets? No one needs this useless piece shit. We don’t want any stupid gimmicky chatbots. We want healthcare. We want affordable gas.Fix the shit you broke. Then we can talk about plagiarism robots.Now here’s a question that doesn’t need fact-checking:Is Missouri Republican Senator Eric Schmitt dumber than a wet carton of dog shit?The answer is, quite obviously, — and yesterday, he went out of his way to prove it, during Jack Smith’s appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee.Check out this smug, smirking asshole. Senator Eric Schmitt (R-MO) launched a hit on Smith, setting up the idea he was part of a conspiracy with Fulton County, Georgia, district attorney Fani Willis and her colleague Nathan Wade to persecute Trump.Schmitt asked Smith: “Did you go to an NBA game between the Golden State Warriors and the Atlanta Hawks on February 3, 2024?”Smith looked confused at the sudden turn in the hearing and asked Schmitt to repeat the question. Once Schmitt did, and asked him if he had ever been to Atlanta during his time as special counsel, Smith answered: “I really don’t think so. It’s possible I flew through the Atlanta airport on the way to Florida, but I do not have a recollection of going to Atlanta. I definitely did not go to a Hawks game. I’m sure of that.”Seriously, Jack Smith is super confused, and the expression on his face is all, ‘what the fuck are you gibbering about?’Then Schmitt pounced: “What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warrior/Hawks game on February 3, 2024, the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” A staffer briefly flashed a poster board. Then Schmitt said: “I don’t think you know that we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t, you know, perjure yourself.”Smith said: “[I]f this is the correct basketball game, I recall going to a University of Maryland basketball game where Caitlin Clark was playing right around that time…. You could check if that was the exact date. It was Maryland playing Iowa, I think, February of 2024.”Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) figured it out. Schmitt was accusing Smith of being in Atlanta at an Atlanta Hawks game, where he could hypothetically have met up with Willis and Wade. In reality, he was in Maryland at a game in which Maryland played the University of Iowa: the Hawkeyes.Holy shit. Eric Schmitt just wasted everyone’s time because neither he nor anyone on his staff were smart enough to understand that the University of Iowa HawkeyesHow do you fuck that shit up?Reading is fundamental, you stupid chowderheads. We all learned that, back in grade school.That sound you just heard was Schmitt stepping on an infinite series of rakes.Shut the fuck up, White House Chatbot.Oh, and here’s the icing on the cake.Newscasters who reviewed tapes of the games found Smith in the stands at the Maryland game.“Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation. If asked whether to prosecute a former president today, based on the same facts, I would do so regardless of whether that president was a Republican or a Democrat. The charges against President Trump were the result of the evidence. Grand juries in two separate districts reached this conclusion based on his actions in the indictments they returned. Rather than accept his defeat in the 2020 presidential election, President Trump engaged in a criminal scheme to overturn the results and prevent the lawful transfer of power.”In a world of dumbfucks like Eric Schmitt, be a Jack Smith.oh hey — it’s time for some Daily Claudia.here are three photos from the patio. first up, Sunday morning bloody marys and brunch, on May 14, 2017next, afternoon martinis on a late-winter day, March 6, 2022.lastly, here’s Ms Spouse, crafting a necklace on June 14, 2022.Have a great Wednesday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Christian Tietze: Watch My EmacsConf Talk: Zettelkasten for Regular Emacs Hackers
item.author: Christian Tietze
item.content:encoded:
Zettelkasten for Regular Emacs Hackers, EmacsConf 2025 (23 minutes)The pitch: writing improves the quality and depth of thought, and a Zettelkasten is an environment for thinking through writing, not merely a place to store notes. Nobody can hand you a finished thinking environment the way they can hand you an email client. You have to build your own, and Emacs is the most moldable place to do it.In 23 minutes, I walk through:the three essential mechanics: (with effort), (with links), and (improve notes as you learn more);the habits that make it scale over decades: design for use, create structure, start in the Zettelkasten, and start with a link;why “garbage in, garbage out” applies to notes, too;This is the whole configuration I used in the demo. Save it as in an empty folder and launch Emacs from there:emacs init.el These are the notes I wrote during the recording. The video runs them at 3 to 4 times the speed, so they’re easier to read here.Mechanics and habits to use a Zettelkasten#+title: Mechanics and habits to use a Zettelkasten #+date: [2025-11-21 Fri 20:48] #+filetags: :zettelkasten: #+identifier: 20251121T204827
Essential: - Write: put in effort; [[denote:20251121T205045][GIGO]] - Connect: Link notes to create trails - Correct: Improve as you go
Additional: - Design for use: give things a purpose, e.g. blog about it - Create structure. [[denote:20251121T205312][Types of structures in a Zettelkasten]]: design new entry points and trails - Start in the Zettelkasten: use the system to learn, make it grow, get better - Start with a link: keeps your notes connected. [[denote:20251121T210416][Create notes as link first to avoid orphans]]
Tool doesn't matter as much. Small files are good. [[denote:20251121T210107][Use Denote in Emacs]]
(Christian Tietze: Zettelkasten for Regular Emacs Hackers, EmacsConf 2025) #+title: Garbage in, garbage out #+date: [2025-11-21 Fri 20:50] #+filetags: :programming:quality: #+identifier: 20251121T205045
The principle known as "Garbage In, Garbage Out" (GIGO) in computer programming states that for any system, the quality of output is directly depending on the quality of input.
See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_in,_garbage_out Types of structures in a Zettelkasten#+title: Types of structures in a Zettelkasten #+date: [2025-11-21 Fri 20:53] #+filetags: :structure:zettelkasten: #+identifier: 20251121T205312
Non-comprehensive list of structures that could be used in a Zettelkasten:
- Opposition pair: 1 note for the pair, 1 note per position/opposition each; pro/contra - Table of contents: list of topics/headings - an outline for a writing project - recreation of a book's contents (so I can write in detail about the book); - Argument: recreation of a distilled form to get to a conclusion; list premises and evidence, and how these support the conclusion - Counter-argument: address parts of the original argument to support another view and test the argument's strength - Table of things - Graphics, like a concept map, Mind-Map, diagram: visually bring elements into a relation, then write about the relation and the elements
Metaphors: - Iceberg: visibile tip with hidden depth; someting that appears small but is large; good metaphor for obstacles - Black box: focus on inputs and outputs, and ignore the 'how' in the middle - e.g. most Emacs Lisp functions (hoping the documentation is good) - [[denote:20251121T205739][Atom, molecule, organism]]: how small parts compose to larger parts, which compose to even larger pieces
(Christian Tietze: Zettelkasten for Regular Emacs Hackers, EmacsConf 2025) Atom, molecule, organism metaphor#+title: Atom, molecule, organism metaphor #+date: [2025-11-21 Fri 20:57] #+filetags: :composition:recursion: #+identifier: 20251121T205739
Atom: smallest part, indivisible elements Molecule: comprised of atoms; structure added to combine elements Organism: comprised of molecules; different level of analysis, irreducible to molecules/atoms
This can be used e.g. for programming: functions compose into larger functions which compose into packages.
Actual biological organisms also work in such a way. Organs are part of bodily functions (high abstraction), but from a chemical or physical perspective, you can decompose them into atoms. That doesn't tell you anything about the organ's function. Denote.el for Zettelkasten in Emacs#+title: Denote.el for Zettelkasten in Emacs #+date: [2025-11-21 Fri 21:01] #+filetags: :denote:emacs:zettelkasten: #+identifier: 20251121T210107
While not shipping with Emacs out of the box, Denote is easy to install and a great start to manage notes:
- it comes with unified way to create new notes, and hides time-stamped ID's with "[D]" in buffer lists - it can manage links, and show incoming links to notes ("backlinks") - it supports quickly adding links, and creating links _first_ out of the box -- it just creates the note immediately, so you don't notice - [[denote:20251121T210416][Create notes as link first to avoid orphans]]
* Example configuration
#+BEGIN_SRC elisp (use-package denote :ensure t :hook (dired-mode . denote-dired-mode) :bind (("C-c n n" . denote) ("C-c n r" . denote-rename-file) ("C-c n l" . denote-link) ("C-c n c" . denote-link-after-creating) ("C-c n b" . denote-backlinks) ("C-c n d" . denote-dired) ("C-c n g" . denote-grep)) :config (setq denote-directory (expand-file-name "./notes/"))
;; Automatically rename Denote buffers when opening them so that ;; instead of their long file name they have, for example, a literal ;; "[D]" followed by the file's title. Read the doc string of ;; `denote-rename-buffer-format' for how to modify this. (denote-rename-buffer-mode 1)) #+END_SRC Create notes as link first to avoid orphans#+title: Create notes as link first to avoid orphans #+date: [2025-11-21 Fri 21:04] #+filetags: :linking:zettelkasten: #+identifier: 20251121T210416
Recommended practice by Christian Tietze: start a new note with a link first from some place, any place, then create the file to match that link (which would initially lead nowhere).
- Reduces orphans in the Zettelkasten by guaranteeing every note to have at least one link. - Supposedly teaches you to think about possible connections early, which makes the network better.
A very loosey-goosey approach, when taken literally and used liberally: it doesn't matter where you are, just leave a forward link to something you wish existed. Even if it doesn't fit the current note. After all, you came up with the idea just now -- so maybe there's a connection that you just can't spell out, yet? If you want the general introduction without Emacs, zettelkasten.de is the place to start.Get new posts delivered to your inbox — subscribe.

item.title: Zumwalt out as Royals hitting coach
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: The Royals press conference to wrap the 2026 season is later on Wednesday. That didn't prevent news about the on-field staff from coming out on Tuesday. Ken Rosenthal at The Athletic had the scoop: The Royals were removing hitting coach Alec Zumwalt from the dugout. Zumwalt just completed his 15th season with the Royals. He has been the Senior Director of Hitting Performance since 2021. He added hitting coach to his duties on May 16, 2022, replacing Terry Bradshaw.Zumwalt came under quite a bit of fire as the offense seemed to regress across the board in 2025 and the Royals faded from the playoff race. The cracks started to show in September of 2024. The fire didn't abate in the early going in 2026 as an underperforming offense in the first two months of the season was part of the Royals three ring circus of baseballing frustrations.Despite the early struggles, the Royals offense ran surprisingly close to league average for most of the 2026 season. They had a good April where they collectively hit .240/.322/.389 which was exactly in line with league average production. The nadir was the following month. In May the Royals hit .228/.294/.356, which was an 82 OPS+. That was abysmal. But they recovered and posted well the rest of the year. From Baseball Reference, we can see the Royals offense was fairly steady once they got past May:Individually, Jac Caglianone really broke out this summer. He was the AL Player of the Month for August. Carter Jensen had an amazing season, building off his impressive cup of coffee from 2025. That culminated with an AL Player of the Month award for September. (More on that in a moment.) If you’re going to put the hitting coach on blast for underperforming players, you have to dole out some credit when the cornerstones of your organization flourish.This is a results-based business. On offense, the results could be measured by the amount of runs scored. Here's how the Royals have done over the last five seasons in runs scored per game, along with their rank in the majors. 2026 - 4.26 R/G (22nd)2025 - 4.02 R/G (26th)2023 - 4.17 R/G (23rd)The 2024 season looks like an extreme outlier but 2026 feels like a step forward. Since overall league offensive production varies from season to season, a full table from FanGraphs helps show how the Royals have done in regards to the league.A reminder that wRC+ is Weighted Runs Created which is kind of a catch-all of offensive performance relative to the league. The league average is always 100. A number above 100 is above league average. Below 100 is below league average. In the Zumwalt hitting coach era, the Royals have run consistently below league average with their strongest years being 2024 and 2026.Look at the raw numbers in the table above. The Royals posted their best walk rate, tied for the most home runs, posted their best OBP and fell just a single point off their high mark for slugging percentage in 2026. Most hitters showed marked improvement after the All-Star Break. Maybe that was the adjustment period fellow hitting coaches Marcus Thames and Connor Dawson, both brought on board prior to the season, needed to begin to make an impact. Zumwalt remains Senior Director of Hitting Performance so I assume the organization hitting philosophy continues to start with him and filters down to the dugout. He will certainly be less hands-on than previously, which could be a good thing. I don't know. Also, how will the Royals ride with their hitting coaches now? Will Dawson or Thames get the bump to the lead hitting coach or will they continue in tandem? They seemed to have developed a strong working relationship with the players. The results in the last four months of the season certainly suggest some progress.What I believe this move signals is that the Royals feel there's more to come from their offensive performance. I can't disagree there, but the club would be better served to finding two or three productive bats from outside the org. The Picollo Era has been marked by awarding too many plate appearances to too many sub-mediocre hitters.Zumwalt has been in the sights for a segment of this fan base for the better part of two seasons. I get it. When a team underperforms—and the Royals have certainly underperformed—there needs to be accountability. Owner John Sherman's guy is Picollo. Picollo's guy is Quatraro. So someone on the coaching staff needs to take the fall. Or be reassigned. For myself, I'm fine with this move. It needed to be made simply because the offensive valleys have been too low for too long and the peaks aren't high enough. A new voice is needed. Or the current voices—other than Zumwalt—need to be amplified. Bringing Thames and Dawson on board were solid moves. This is an opportunity to maximize the returns.It's too bad this news broke about 24 hours before Picollo and Quatraro were scheduled to meet the media because that means we're spending a full day just speculating as to what it all means. I imagine this will be topic number one on Wednesday.There will most certainly be more to come.As noted earlier, MLB announced their monthly honors on Tuesday with Carter Jensen bringing home a couple of pieces of hardware. Jensen bagged the AL Player of the Month award and was also named the AL Rookie of the Month. Nice haul.Jensen’s September was dreamy. In 21 games covering 80 PAs, he hit .338/.407/.787 with 10 doubles, eight homers and 20 RBI. Those 10 doubles were the most in the majors in September. He also led the league in extra-base hits (he tossed in one triple for good measure), slugging percentage and OPS.I think for all of us, the most impressive part of Jensen’s month was his streak where 12 straight hits went for extra bases. That’s now a major league record for a rookie, previously held by Aaron Judge.Just for fun—and a little perspective—I visited Stathead to find the best months in Royals history as ranked by OPS. Here are the top 15:There are some franchise icons on that list. Impressive.What left me kind of shocked was the note from the Royals PR team that Jensen was the first primary catcher in club history to win an AL Player of the Month award. I figure most of you will think immediately about Salvador Perez, but us elder statesmen would pivot to Darrell Porter, who had an outstanding season behind the plate for the Royals in 1979.For fun, I took the query from Stathead above and filtered to highlight the catchers. Normally, I'd do top 10 because that's what you do. I decided to expand the list by one to help highlight the insane '79 season Porter had.Gotta say I did not expect to see Gregg Zaun on the list. Twice!But look at Jensen at the second-best month for a catcher in franchise history sorted by OPS. And it's the top OPS+, meaning, like wRC+ it's adjusted for league performance. He's not going to win the Rookie of the Year award, but that shouldn't diminish the impressive season he just completed. The kid is a dude.

item.title: Across the Horizon Ep. 71: Lara Somogyi
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: On today’s episode of Across the Horizon, host Bob Holmes of the band SUSS is joined by Lara Somogyi. Lara is a harpist and composer who recently released an album on Mercury KX Records. They talk about her new music as well as the playlist of ambient music that she brought to the show, including Ólafur Arnalds, Clarice Jensen, Steve Reich, Koki Nakano, and much more.For Flow State, we’re listening to two albums by Somogyi, whose music has appeared on many of our mixes and whom we featured last year. First up is the new record, , on which she passes her harp through a medley of effects pedals. She says on the show, “I’ve been listening to a lot of music that shifts time for me, or makes me feel time physically. I started making the record because I was curious about time… I discovered I experience it through sensory markers rather than through numerical markers.” We’re also playing from last year, a collaboration with Joshua Tree-born pianist Jean-Michel Blais. Included in our daily playlist for paying subscribers is her unmissable covers of “Running Up That Hill” and “Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence,” among other selections.

item.title: Hump Day Hottie: Leni Klum
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Leni Klum is a German-American model who has developed her own career in fashion while growing up in the public eye. Born May 4, 2004, in New York City, she is the daughter of supermodel and television personality Heidi Klum and Italian businessman Flavio Briatore. Leni was raised primarily by her mother and stepfather, musician Seal, and later began pursuing modeling professionally.She made her modeling debut alongside Heidi Klum in a 2020 cover and fashion editorial for Vogue Germany, quickly attracting attention as the daughter of one of the fashion industry’s most recognizable figures. Since then, Leni has appeared in campaigns and editorials for major fashion and beauty brands and has walked in runway shows. Her work has included appearances for Dolce & Gabbana and other prominent designers.While her family background has naturally generated media interest, Leni has increasingly established herself as a model in her own right. With her distinctive look, growing fashion portfolio, and international exposure, she represents a new generation of celebrity-connected models.

item.title: Rusty Red State Candidates With Rusty Values
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: This afternoon I saw an ad being run by a SuperPAC supporting Dan Osborn (“Nebraska Values PAC”) against Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) of Nebraska. It’s a brutal ad about a brutal crime. (You can watch it here.) A woman identified as “Jody S.” speaks over a montage of a crime scene imagery explaining that in 1993 an intruder broke into her home, tied her to her bed and violently raped her while her children listened to everything. A man named John Arias was arrested, pled guilty, was convicted and sentenced to prison. We then fast-forward to then-Gov. Pete Ricketts casting the deciding vote as the member of a pardon board that ultimately pardoned Arias. Jody S. notes that Arias told her she would never be safe from him and that he was now off the state sex offender registry and allowed to own a gun. She also notes that she wasn’t even informed about the pardon until after it happened.I tend to be hard-hearted about political ads. I watched this one a few times to make sure I had the details right. It’s hard to watch; in a way it’s more hard to listen to. The ad has stark black and white imagery and has audio of Ricketts announcing, in an uncomfortably chipper tone, his vote during the hearing: “But with that you’ve got your pardon.”

item.title: I am comfortable living in Linux, but...
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: After many failed attempts, I am finally comfortable doing all of my computing using Linux. In case you haven't heard, Linux is good now! And yet, I'm back on my Mac...for now.The short version? It's the software. Linux is loaded with pretty good apps, many of them free. Thing is, nearly all of them also run on macOS. This means that on a Mac, I can use all the great macOS software, and most of the great apps I use on Linux..I've spent the past year recreating the dozens of little workflows on Linux that I'd built for myself on the Mac. Some of them were easily portable, but many weren't. Some had no real replacements, so I had to give them up.The things I like about Linux are abstract. The "I'm in complete control of my computing environment" kind of things. I miss that feeling on the Mac, especially when I can't launch an app that I downloaded or when I've had to dismiss the two thousandth permissions dialog that day. Also, I love the "This twelve-year-old ThinkPad still works great running Linux!"What I don't miss are all the Linux distros. I mean, what an embarrassment of riches, right? Except my brain never stops thinking "What if I switched to...?" every other day. Half the time I actually have switched, with disastrous effects on my time. I don't enjoy the community bickering either. "Systemd sucks!" and so on. And there's still too much "Um, actually..." and "Why don't you just...?"Overall, my year-long adventure with Linux was fun and successful. But I don't want to give up some of the Mac software I've used for years...sometimes years.What might be the biggest draw of macOS for me is that I automatically get Emacs key bindings everywhere. I hadn't realized how much I relied on them until they were gone.I'm sure I'll revisit this again at some point. I still have a couple of nice laptops running Linux, and I'll certainly pop them open occasionally, but for now, I'm going to live on my Mac.I know some of you have been rooting for me to fully adopt Linux. Please don't be too disappointed. Everything with me is temporary :). At least I know I can switch completely to Linux if I want to. I'm just not ready.
